items.content: Policy AI Tech Wikipedia’s operator says a bad AI copyright ruling could threaten the open web In the NYT’s case against OpenAI, the Wikimedia Foundation says training AI should be fair use — but regurgitating articles shouldn’t. In the NYT’s case against OpenAI, the Wikimedia Foundation says training AI should be fair use — but regurgitating articles shouldn’t. by Lauren Feiner Oct 30, 2026, 9:00 AM UTC Image: The Verge Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform. The Wikimedia Foundation is staking out a middle ground in a group of landmark AI copyright cases, pushing courts to legally protect large language models (LLMs) training on copyrighted work — but not chatbots regurgitating that work to users. An overly black-and-white ruling, it says, could either deprive Wikipedians of useful AI-based tools or endanger the open web. In an amicus brief filed Friday, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia weighed in on a set of lawsuits pitting publishers including The New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft, taking neither side. “Wikimedia is concerned that the parties’ positions in this case push for overbroad and simplified applications of the fair use doctrine” around AI, the organization says in its legal filing. A nuance-free victory for publishers, it fears, could let copyright holders “gatekeep” even innovative and transformative uses of their work. On the other hand, a victory for AI companies could constitute “a green light to snub licensing terms and fragment the flow of knowledge between human authors and audiences.” “Wikimedia is concerned that the parties’ positions in this case push for overbroad and simplified applications of the fair use doctrine” The ruling could be existential for Wikipedia. Wikimedia websites “have become one of the most critical sources of data for all artificial intelligence and machine learning training,” the company says in the filing. But these same systems siphon away visitors , undermining the communities that maintain these sites. Wikimedia argues that they’re also violating copyright: services like ChatGPT reproduce text that’s licensed freely under Creative Commons, it says, but don’t adhere to the terms of that license. At the same time, it says, the large language models that power these systems are useful to Wikipedia: they can help editors fight vandalism, detect copyright violations and doxxing, and look for articles that need improvement, among other uses. “A ruling that does not apply fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge, and stifle the development of open source technologies, ultimately impacting access to information for everyone in both cases,” Wikimedia Foundation general council Stephen LaPorte says in a statement. “The court needs to understand that Wikipedia is created through a collaborative process that requires a strong foundation of open and accessible human knowledge to thrive.” “A ruling that does not apply fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge” The Times argues for a more expansive definition of fair use as it applies to LLMs. It alleges , for example, that OpenAI infringed on its copyright by scraping its website to build training datasets. OpenAI and Microsoft both contend that using LLMs constitutes fair use. OpenAI has said that regurgitating work “is a rare bug.” Microsoft, in a September filing , says that expert analysis found that Copilot rarely reproduces full sentences from news content used to ground the model, which it said, “hardly undermines the transformative purpose of LLM training.” Wikimedia proposes a compromise. Scraping websites shouldn’t be considered copyright infringement, it argues, and using copyrighted works to pre-train LLMs without a license should constitute fair use when they provide “something new and different from the original sources,” according to a blog post. But if these models pull copies of material in response to user queries, then deliver it to users “while supplanting readers’ engagement with those original works,” that should require a license. The key difference is that in the latter case, AI output is simply substituting for the original work, and doesn’t transform it enough to qualify as fair use. In those cases, Wikimedia says that AI companies should respect licensing requirements to use such information. For Wikipedia, this would mean crediting the original source of information under its Creative Commons license, which also requires “any remix or adaptations” to remain under that same license. “We are taking a position in this case to defend the free and open human knowledge that Wikipedia depends on,” Wikimedia CEO Bernadette Meehan says in a statement. “Expanding access to knowledge through AI is a powerful goal, but it must respect the people, contributors, and communities that make reliable knowledge possible. Finding this balance is both a mutual benefit and a shared responsibility for the entire information ecosystem.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon: Our next frontier model
items.content: Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model Oct 28, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon. Posted in:

items.fingerprint: mistral releases weights for its trillion parameter ai model targeting cybersecurity|techcrunch.com/2026/10
items.title: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity
items.description: Mistral says its new model can afford organizations a kind of control over its cyber defenses that closed models can't.
items.content: French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month . The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems. Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.” The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes. Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3. The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site. “Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.” The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API. Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves. “Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Access that can’t be cut off by definition because the model is open-weighted,” he said. Stock added that the model could be used to “identify, coordinate, and respond in real time to major security incidents, and that the open sourcing means that companies can deploy this model on-prem in their own ecosystem. While advances in AI cybersecurity are helping security professionals to find bugs at a much higher rate than before, Stock continued, he believes it’s important for companies to “provide [this same] capability to everyone…as soon as possible to ramp up and to strengthen the ecosystem,” given that “some malicious actors might try to actually leverage their own technology to attack.” Separately, Stock addressed concerns about recent incidents involving rogue AI agents, acknowledging the risks but cautioning against overreacting. “We don’t want to fearmonger people. We think it’s a problem that is solvable. It’s a hard problem to have good security,” he said. Lucas Ropek Senior Writer, TechCrunch Lucas is a senior writer at TechCrunch, where he covers artificial intelligence, consumer tech, and startups. He previously covered AI and cybersecurity at Gizmodo. You can contact Lucas by emailing [email protected] . View Bio

items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software Enterprise Article Published October 29, 2026 Upvote 12 +6 Kate Soule katesoule Follow ibm-granite Luis A Lastras GrizleeBer Follow ibm-granite Subhajit Chaudhury subhajit1412 Follow ibm-granite Abraham Daniels abedaniels Follow ibm-granite :last-child]:mb-0"> Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1 , showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint. Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. Until then, test out our latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo. items.title: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 41 +35 merve merve Follow Alvaro Bartolome alvarobartt Follow Rémi Ouazan Reboul ror Follow Cyril Vallez cyrilvallez Follow Quentin Gallouédec qgallouedec Follow Enrique Hernández Calabrés ehcalabres Follow Juan Julián juanjucm Follow Xuan-Son Nguyen ngxson Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Aritra Roy Gosthipaty ariG23498 Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter , and a context window of 1M tokens . The model is released in two official variants: FP8 NVFP4 There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings). Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more! Table of Contents "Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face" Table of Contents What is new with Mistral Large 4 Cybersecurity Capabilities Architecture Vision encoder Benchmark Results Inference Support Transformers vLLM Llama.cpp Fine-tuning with TRL Inference Endpoints Dell Enterprise Hub Try it out What is new with Mistral Large 4 Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions. You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection . Cybersecurity Capabilities Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for. Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model. For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description. In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community. We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here . Architecture Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query. For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers. The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token. Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope , a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency. Vision encoder Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below. Benchmark Results Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index. On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1 , 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA , and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4 . Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max. Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase , which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks. Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance: Artificial Analysis Cyber Index: ML4 ranks among the top five models globally on this independent evaluation of models’ ability to find and fix software vulnerabilities. Vulnerability reproduction and patching: It achieves 82% , the highest reported score on this test within the index. The task requires reproducing a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patching it, testing both investigation and remediation. Cybench: ML4 solves 93% of a suite of 40 challenges drawn from security competitions , demonstrating strong performance on hands-on security problems. Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark , adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation. Inference Support Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team . We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers. Transformers The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM , with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low , medium , high as reasoning effort. The default is high , and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort : none would still use high . To run the model, upgrade the transformers package pip install --upgrade transformers import os from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM, DistributedConfig distributed_config = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ) model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, distributed_config=distributed_config, ) # only text text_messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Who are you?" } ] # text + image multimodal_messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/cats-image/resolve/main/cats_image.jpeg" , }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "How many cats are in the image?" , }, ], }, ] for messages in [text_messages, multimodal_messages]: inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 100 ) if int (os.environ[ "RANK" ]) == 0 : print (processor.decode(outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], skip_special_tokens= False )) You can run the script above by saving it in a python file script.py and then run torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 script.py vLLM vLLM supports the high-quality NVFP4 Mistral Large 4 checkpoint, which has a smaller memory footprint and requires NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. The model also ships with a DSpark drafter for additional speed-ups with vLLM. Launch the server like this: vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \ --config-format mistral \ --load-format mistral \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --decode-context-parallel-size 8 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --enforce-eager \ --mm_processor_cache_gb 0.0 Once the server is up and running, you can run the following. curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 17*23?"}],"max_tokens":512}' Llama.cpp Llama.cpp and Llama App already support Mistral Large 4. You can install Llama App with the following command: curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh Then you can start the server as follows, indicating the quant suffix after the model ID: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF:Q2_K Here’s the repository with the quants derived from the FP8 checkpoint, and this is the NVFP4 one , converted from the official NVFP4 repo. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat using the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more. curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ] }' You can run image-text inference as follows. curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer " \ -d '{ "model": "muse-spark-open", "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "What is in this image?" }, { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "data:image/png;base64,..." } } ] } ], "temperature": 0 }' The llama.cpp team ships the following quants: IQ2_XXS , Q2_K , Q4_K_M , NVFP4 , Q8_0 , and BF16 for further conversions. The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards. Running Q2_K on a single M3 Ultra, we got a prefill throughput of about 90 tokens per second, and a generation speed of 15 tok/s. On 4 x RTX6000 Pro, we observed the following results: NVFP4: 32K context size, prefill 130-590 t/s, gen speed ~10 t/s IQ2_XXS: 800K context size. At short context sizes, prefill is 500 tok/s and generation runs at 30 tok/s. However, using long contexts performance drops to 129 tok/s (prefill) and 3 tok/s (generation). Fine-tuning with TRL We also ship day 0 support of fine tuning Mistral Large 4 using TRL. All you have to do is upgrade to the latest version of transformers , trl and peft . pip install --upgrade transformers trl peft In the following example we train the model to perform multilingual thinking. The fine tuned model would be able to reason in the language the system prompt asks for! The script runs on the FP8 variant on a node of 8xB300s. The full example, with a Slurm launcher, is in TRL's examples . # torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 sft.py import os from datasets import load_dataset from peft import LoraConfig from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, DistributedConfig from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer world_size = int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]) model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B" model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained( model_id, distributed_config=DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=world_size, ep_size=world_size), dtype= "auto" , ) dataset = load_dataset( "HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking" , split= "train" ) # the assistant turns carry reasoning, so render them in reasoning mode dataset = dataset. map ( lambda x: { "chat_template_kwargs" : { "reasoning_effort" : "high" }}) trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model, args=SFTConfig( packing= True , max_length= 4096 , assistant_only_loss= True , learning_rate= 1e-4 , lr_scheduler_type= "cosine" , warmup_steps= 10 , ), train_dataset=dataset, peft_config=LoraConfig( r= 16 , lora_alpha= 32 , target_modules= r".*language_model.*\.(q_proj|kv_a_proj_with_mqa|kv_b_proj|o_proj|gate_proj|up_proj|down_proj)" , ), ) trainer.train() Inference Endpoints Mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. It serves up to 131K tokens of context and processes up to 16 requests at a time, and we observed the following results: Single request: time to first token of about 0.6 seconds for a 1K-token prompt, and a generation speed of ~65 tok/s, reaching 120–138 tok/s on chat prompts where DSpark's drafts are accepted. Long prompts: 16K-token prompts, four at a time, are prefilled at about 4,300 tok/s in total, with a time to first token of 8–9 seconds. Under load: about 480 tok/s of total generation across 1,000 ShareGPT conversations. You can deploy it with the hf CLI as follows: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B --name mistral-large-4 Once the endpoint is running, you can query its OpenAI-compatible API, using the endpoint URL and your Hugging Face token. The reasoning_effort field controls how much the model reasons before answering, and can be set to low , medium , or high (default). curl " $(hf endpoints describe mistral-large-4 --json | jq -r .status.url) /v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(hf auth token 2>/dev/null) " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ], "reasoning_effort": "medium" }' The answer comes back in choices[0].message.content , and the reasoning in choices[0].message.reasoning . The endpoint also supports tool calls, structured outputs, image inputs, and streaming through the standard Chat Completions fields. Dell Enterprise Hub The easiest way to get up and running with your Dell AI Servers (NVIDIA H200, B200, GB200 or GB300) is by installing the dell-ai CLI: pip install dell-ai && dell-ai login And use it to run an optimized recipe for Mistral Large 4 on e.g., a NVIDIA B300 node. dell-ai models deploy --model-id mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \ --engine docker \ --platform-id xe9780-nvidia-b300 \ --gpus 4 You can find more about this release in the Dell Enterprise Hub (DEH) . Try it out Grab the weights from the Mistral Large 4 collection , run them locally with the GGUFs , or deploy them with Inference Endpoints. We can't wait to see what you build with Le Chonk. Share your fine-tunes, quants and other artefacts on the Hub! items.title: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 10 +4 Mattt mattt Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do. Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive. In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap , we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model. Today we're announcing two packages: AnySpeechRecognizer implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine, including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML, and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when. AnyDecisionModel answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions with typed results and probabilities. It derives each answer from the model's probabilities instead of generating text, using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp, or a decision model from Jev or Ollama. Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device. AnySpeechRecognizer Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer , Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen. It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine: - import Speech + import AnySpeechRecognizer The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer , SpeechTranscriber , DictationTranscriber , SpeechDetector , and AssetInventory , with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber: let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber ( model: ParakeetSpeechModel (variant: .v3), transcriptionOptions: [], reportingOptions: [.volatileResults], attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange] ) The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework. Meet the models Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 . It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale. Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3 . It was more accurate in most of our measurements. Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet . All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence. Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one: let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber ( model: QwenSpeechModel (variant: .large, language: Locale . Language (identifier: "yue" )), transcriptionOptions: [], reportingOptions: [], attributeOptions: [] ) Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input. To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started. Core ML models on the Hub To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub: Model Core ML conversion Original checkpoint License Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 mattt/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-coreml nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 CC BY 4.0 Parakeet Ultra mattt/parakeet-ultra-coreml moondream/parakeet-ultra CC BY 4.0 Parakeet Unified EN 0.6B mattt/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-coreml nvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b NVIDIA Open Model License Qwen3-ASR 0.6B mattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf Apache 2.0 Qwen3-ASR 1.7B mattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coreml Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf Apache 2.0 Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2 CC BY 4.0 Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2.1 mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2.1-coreml nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1 NVIDIA Open Model License Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model. Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools. Speaker diarization When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline: let diarizer = SpeakerDiarizer (model: SortformerDiarizationModel ()) if let request = try await AssetInventory .assetInstallationRequest( supporting: [transcriber, diarizer] ) { try await request.downloadAndInstall() } let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer (modules: [transcriber, diarizer]) The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today. The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1 , which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too. How well does it work? We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes: Transcriber test-clean test-other Parakeet v3, file 1.55% 2.78% Parakeet v3, live 4.73% 4.29% Parakeet Ultra, file 1.66% 2.55% Parakeet Ultra, live 2.65% 3.28% Parakeet Unified, file 1.43% 2.19% Parakeet Unified, live 1.45% 2.42% Apple's transcriber, file 2.12% 3.97% Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%. These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements . So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone. Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27. AnyDecisionModel AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly. It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification. What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them. Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives. Here's what a decision looks like in Swift: import AnyDecisionModel enum Department : String , Choosable { case billing, technical, sales } let ticket = "I was charged twice for my order, and now the app logs me out when I try to ask for a refund." let model = MLXDecisionModel (modelID: "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit" ) let session = DecisionSession (model: model, state: .text(ticket)) let urgent = try await session.probability(of: "Does this convey urgency?" ) let team = try await session.choice( "Which team?" , from: Department . self ) let anger = try await session.score( "How frustrated?" , levels: [ "Calm" , "Frustrated" , "Very angry" ] ) urgent is a Double . team is a Choice<Department> containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable , team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch . If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch. For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass. Try it out: Emoji Magnet Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back. The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example: Statement: a heavy winter coat fits the description "things you wear". Is this statement true? The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY , the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive. Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository. Decision heads and Clef Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant. AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX: let model = MLXHeadDecisionModel ( modelID: "mlx-community/clef-flash-4bit" , head: .jointSchema ) You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states. Calibrating and checking probabilities Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration , which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results. Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation. Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere. Backends AnyDecisionModel has six backends: MLX runs a small language model on Apple silicon with mlx-swift-lm and downloads it from the Hub. MLX decision heads run a model with its own trained decision head, such as Clef. Core AI does the same as MLX with a Core AI model on macOS 27 and iOS 27. llama.cpp reads decisions from a local GGUF model through llama.swift . Jev calls TypeSafe's Jev through the System One API , or any server that implements it, such as Kev . Ollama calls a System One decision model on a local Ollama server or in Ollama's cloud. It requires Ollama 0.35.0 or later, or 0.40.5 or later for cloud models. The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit. Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX , CoreAI , or Llama trait for the local backends. Get started Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime. Add the packages to your Package.swift : dependencies: [ .package(url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer" , from: "0.1.0" ), .package( url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnyDecisionModel" , from: "0.6.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ), ] For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x. Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear , that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple , --backend parakeet , or --backend qwen ; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets. Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories. Links AnySpeechRecognizer on GitHub AnyDecisionModel on GitHub AnyDecisionModel-Examples on GitHub AnyLanguageModel on GitHub swift-huggingface on GitHub Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow. items.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
items.description: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings is buying ADT in a $15.3 billion deal, with plans to bring AI to the home security business.
items.content: In Brief Posted: 12:56 PM PDT · October 29, 2026 Image Credits: Timon Schneider/SOPA Images/LightRocket / Getty Images Julie Bort OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said. Thrive Holdings is the holding company spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner , as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says. As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies. Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said. AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras . ADT already partners with Apple and Google and is expected to continue to do so. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards . Note: This story was updated to include ADT’s current partnerships and to describe Thrive Holdings as a holding company. items.title: Deepgram acquires Pipecat-maker Daily to bolster its voice AI infrastructure
items.description: With Pipecat, Deepgram will likely gain a deeper understanding of real-time voice and video infrastructure.
items.content: The voice AI sector is hot, and top players are trying to consolidate their position as more business models come to the fore through partnerships and acquisitions. Deepgram is the latest to make such moves: The company said on Thursday that it is acquiring Daily, the maker and maintainer of one of the most popular open source voice AI infrastructures, Pipecat. The companies didn’t disclose the deal amount but said that they will keep Pipecat open source. For the uninitiated, Pipecat is a framework that manages voice and video streams along with other pieces in the pipeline, like speech-to-text (STT), large language models (LLMs), and text-to-speech (TTS) models while reducing latency. Its maker, Daily, provides hosted infrastructure for voice and video calls of any kind. With Pipecat, Deepgram will likely gain a deeper understanding of real-time voice and video infrastructure. Daily has raised over $62 million in funding to date from investors such as Tiger Global, Highfield Capital, Nat Friedman, Lachy Groom, and Kevin Weil, according to PitchBook data. Earlier this year, Deepgram reached unicorn status with a $130 million Series C round . Incidentally, both companies were in the same Y Combinator batch in 2016. Kwindla Kramer, Daily’s co-founder, said around the time when GPT-4 came out, the company started experimenting with AI-to-human communication over voice and text, which eventually resulted in the Pipecat framework. He noted that while there has been a lot of acquisition interest, he favored Deepgram’s CEO Scott Stephenson’s commitment to keeping Pipecat open source forever, and the engineering culture of both organizations matched, giving Daily’s team the freedom to work on different parts of the stack within a bigger organization. “Scott was super committed to Pipecat being open source and vendor-neutral forever. I think there is both a personal commitment and commercial driver there. If you sit in the middle of an ecosystem that’s growing very fast, and have many parts of that ecosystem that are genuinely the best from your company, then everything being as open as possible is like a commercial advantage,” Kramer told TechCrunch. Stephenson said that Deepgram has been wanting to work in open source for a long time, and the company realized that an orchestration framework for agents was a potential area, which drove the decision to partner with Daily. “We want to open up the ecosystem so everybody can build voice agents. It’s great if you’re using Deepgram models, but I want you to be using the best models for your use case. And if Deepgram notices that we have some ground to catch up on in a certain area for our own models and products, that’s great. We want you to use partners, and then we’ll also work on becoming better in those areas,” he said. Stephenson said the acquisition lets developers build agents with expressivity and end-to-end speech systems by plugging in different models and a context bus that connects all parts. For Deepgram, the deal also lets it explore areas beyond voice through Pipecat, as the framework caters to real-time communication in different formats. “We never thought about Pipecat as a voice toolkit. We thought about it as the toolkit we needed to build this new kind of AI-native software. Because of where we came from, we just always assumed real-time,” Kramer said. Deepgram is also launching Real-Time Context Standard (RCS), an open protocol for voice agents that it co-developed with the Pipecat team. The protocol defines metadata like context from the audio, like a whisper, instructions for a language model on how it can use those signals, and guidance on how the response should sound. Voice AI has seen a lot of investment from both the model and the infrastructure sides. Model makers like ElevenLabs , Gradium , and Fish Audio have raised millions of dollars. On the other hand, infrastructure companies like LiveKit and Vapi have raised multimillion-dollar funding rounds this year. items.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
items.description: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility. Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today. As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine , we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability : the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely. Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important. With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions. The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken. Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from. Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it. OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized . The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people. Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used. No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety. AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist. Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research. No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too. Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance. Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.
