The coalition, made up largely of labor and environmental groups, was founded in the wake of the CHIPS and Science Act, which designated $52.7 billion in funding for domestic semiconductor manufacturing. Its goal is to ensure that communities, not corporations, reap the benefits of the tech boom. Semiconductor manufacturing involves the use of hundreds of different per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, which are commonly referred to as forever chemicals because they don’t naturally break down. The durability of these chemicals means they won’t be degraded during the manufacturing process, which can involve hundreds or even thousands of steps. But the qualities that make PFAS so essential to chipmaking are precisely what make them so dangerous to people. Some researchers have linked forever chemicals to liver and kidney issues, high cholesterol, birth defects, and various cancers. The use of forever chemicals isn’t limited to chip manufacturing, or to the tech industry writ large — PFAS have been found in nonstick pans, dental floss, shampoo, menstrual care products, food packaging, and even food itself — but the semiconductor industry, by nature of the manufacturing process, uses a significant amount of chemicals that are detrimental to human health. Some researchers have linked chip manufacturing to thyroid and liver diseases, fertility problems, and cancer — an especially ironic outcome, given AI boosters’ claims that the technology will cure cancer within our lifetimes. Women who worked in chip fabs during the ’80s manufacturing heyday were twice as likely to suffer miscarriages than women who didn’t, and their children were also more likely to experience birth defects. And because each step of semiconductor manufacturing requires thousands of gallons of water, these chemicals ultimately become liquid waste. A single fab can produce tens or hundreds of thousands of gallons of wastewater a day, discharge one bimolecular researcher described as a veritable “soup” of forever chemicals. Traditional wastewater treatment methods often fail to detect forever chemicals, and most semiconductor manufacturers aren’t required to monitor or test for PFAS. Compounding the problem, the exact chemical cocktails used in chip fabs are closely guarded trade secrets. But TSMC says it has “continuously optimized” its in-house PFAS detection systems and is developing technologies to remove PFAS from its wastewater streams. The company also says it’s studying how and when it can use non-PFAS alternatives in the manufacturing process. And Porter pointed out that unlike Tucson, where groundwater has been contaminated by military bases and manufacturing, Phoenix doesn’t have much of a PFAS problem, and city leaders are interested in keeping it that way. Phoenix requires TSMC to treat its water before putting it back into the municipal wastewater system, Porter said. And all Arizona cities are required to comply with standards set by the Environmental Protection Agency. Still, for organizers like Barish, wastewater disposal remains a concern. While TSMC and other chip manufacturers have to comply with city and EPA standards, Donald Trump has largely defanged the EPA and eased restrictions on PFAS in drinking water since returning to office. But concessions for chip manufacturers have been largely bipartisan. The Building Chips in America Act — sponsored by Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) and signed into law by President Joe Biden — exempted semiconductor manufacturing from key environmental review. Arizonans have gone to great lengths to reduce their water consumption and to roll back the industrial pollution that has tainted groundwater in Tucson and surrounding communities for decades. Still, experts say the mess caused by PFAS could take generations to clean up . And as the state’s economy becomes increasingly tied to tech — which not only uses huge amounts of water but also produces industrial waste — some residents fear an even more parched Arizona, a drought exacerbated by the promise of industry. The culprit there isn’t population growth or heavy industry, at least not in the way most people think of it. It’s agriculture Arizona’s historic megadrought was set in motion well before any part of the tech industry gained a foothold in the Grand Canyon State. It’s an almost cartoonishly simple issue of supply and demand, one whose consequences are complex and still uncertain. Hotter and drier summers in the Rocky Mountains are drying up the Colorado River, the source of more than one-third of Arizona’s water. At the same time, Arizona’s aquifers are being drained far faster than they can be replenished. The latter is a problem of demand, the former one of supply. Together, they add up to a crisis over a century in the making. The 1922 Colorado River Compact — the agreement that determines how much of the river’s water to allocate to seven states — simultaneously overestimated the long-term supply of water and underestimated the demand. Legislators in 1922 could not have foreseen the midcentury population boom or the severity of climate change. But this alone does not explain Arizona’s current water woes. There’s also the matter of Arizona’s dwindling aquifers. The culprit there isn’t population growth or heavy industry, at least not in the way most people think of it. It’s agriculture, an extractive, hyperindustrialized process unto itself. Arizona’s now romanticized five C’s were largely brought to the state from elsewhere, and they continue to use far more water than a casual observer imagines or expects. You can’t grow cotton and citrus in the desert, nor can you raise cattle, without water — lots of it. Over the past decade, one commodity crop, increasingly dominated by hedge funds and foreign investors, has become a sort of scapegoat for the state’s water woes: alfalfa. Its presence is incongruous and inescapable, shocks of green in a sea of clay. Every few dozen miles, the earth-toned monotony that surrounds I-10, the artery connecting Tucson and Phoenix, is interrupted by fields of the stuff. The plant — technically a legume — is grown as cow feed, fueling one of the state’s oldest and most romanticized industries. More recently, however, deep-pocketed outsiders started getting in on the game, growing alfalfa to produce hay for herds overseas. Until 2011, almost all of Arizona’s alfalfa crop was consumed inside the state. And then Fondomonte moved in. Image 1 of 3 An alfalfa field along Interstate 10 in Arizona. The active management area comprised about 326,000 acre-feet in 2024, most of which was slated for residential use. And yet it’s not AI safety, air pollution, or fears of AGI-enabled economic collapse but water that dominates the data center debate in Arizona and elsewhere, even when those other issues are raised, too. More broadly, recent concerns over data centers’ water usage may stem from Empire of AI , a 2025 bestseller by journalist Karen Hao that traces the rise of OpenAI — and, for all its journalistic merits, significantly overestimates one data center’s water usage by a factor of 1,000. Partly in response to Hao’s book, and to the widespread backlash to data center construction, the AI industry has gone on the defensive, but hardly anyone is buying what they’re selling, even when they’re telling the truth. It’s easy to make fun of Sam Altman’s self-exculpatory assertion that it takes more water to grow a single almond than to make 38,000 ChatGPT queries, or to quibble with his lazy math, but the general sentiment is nonetheless true. Globally, agriculture uses about 70 percent of the world’s fresh water; the same is true in Arizona, though agriculture accounted for just 0.4 percent of the state’s gross domestic product in 2023. One could argue that, unlike data centers, farms are necessary for human life — although most of the crops grown around the world are used for biofuels, or to feed livestock , not people. But many locals maintain that any amount of water used for AI is too much. The No Desert Data Center Coalition encourages Arizonans to look beyond the issue of water, tying its fight against Project Blue to a bigger, more fraught battle against extractive industry in all its forms, urging the state and local governments to prioritize industries that revitalize the land instead of further destroying it. Coalition members describe data centers as crucial infrastructure that powers the “cruelty industry,” emphasizing the connections between tech, mass surveillance, and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Still, the broader opposition to data centers seemingly always comes back to water. The concern is especially acute in the drought-stricken state, which lost up to one-third of its Colorado River allotment in late August. Tucson, which sources about 70 percent of its water from the Colorado River, has been preparing for this moment for years. Since 2003, the city has used its excess Colorado River water, which flows to the city through a 326-mile network of aqueducts, to recharge the Avra Valley aquifer . Tucson recently expanded its groundwater treatment plant, opening a dedicated facility to cleanse the aquifer of forever chemicals. Through its conservation efforts, Tucson has banked enough groundwater to sustain its residents for an estimated 47 years, but locals say that water should be used for them and their families, not to enrich tech companies in California. The opposition to Project Blue has rallied around a succinct slogan: NOT ONE DROP FOR DATA. “This Town Council has never met a development they didn’t like” Widespread opposition has done little to temper Beale’s ambitions. In the midst of the Project Blue saga, news broke that the developer was looking into building a data center campus in Marana, a rural town 20 miles northwest of Tucson. Beale submitted an application to the Town Council last October, asking it to rezone two adjoining 300-acre plots. One of the properties was owned by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The other belongs to a trust connected to Herb Kai, a member of the Town Council who boasts more than three decades in public service. The Kais are the biggest landowners in town. The patriarch, Cantonese immigrant John Kai, moved to Marana in the 1930s. John, whose descendants remember him as savvy and tenacious, evaded the racist federal ban on Chinese immigrants by assuming a new identity. In Marana, he earned a living hauling vegetables to and from Tucson for the town’s farmers. Eventually he had enough money to buy a plot of his own, where he cultivated cotton. Kai slowly built up his holdings and diversified his investments, and in so doing helped transform once-sleepy Marana into a bustling little town. It is now one of the fastest-growing communities in southern Arizona. Its population has increased by nearly 25 percent since 2020, now hovering around 65,000, but its leaders still think there’s plenty of room to grow. The town is nearly three times the size of Boston and has one-tenth of the population — at least for now. “You’ll talk to people and they’ll say this Town Council has never met a development they didn’t like,” Marana resident Jackie McGuire told me. McGuire, a cybersecurity analyst, moved to Marana from California 15 years ago. She still misses the near-perfect climate of the Bay Area and the easy access to the best Vietnamese food in the country, and her bright pink hair looks out of place in the town, where most people are conservative and many are Mormon. But she loves the desert and the life she has built there. And now the Town Council, she said, is poised to destroy exactly what drew her to Marana in the first place. Though she had never been involved in local politics, McGuire was one of dozens of Marana residents to speak out against Beale’s proposal at a Town Council meeting in December. Photo: Nicky Woo for The Verge Jackie McGuire, described by some as a “liberal with pink hair,” found herself elected to Marana’s Town Council on an anti-data center platform. “I had my children here. I’m raising my children here,” McGuire said. “The town has done a phenomenal job of creating public spaces where people want to come out of their houses and socialize.” The data center, she said, would be an “eyesore,” but her opposition to it isn’t purely aesthetic. McGuire, who worked on Wall Street in the years leading up to the Great Recession, is worried that the AI bubble is about to burst. “One thing I find curious that Beale hasn’t mentioned is that they’re a subsidiary of a company called Blue Owl,” which is currently embroiled in a class action lawsuit for securities fraud, McGuire said. “For what it’s worth,” she added, “I make a living on cloud computing. This AI bubble bursting is going to materially impact my ability to pay my mortgage, and I will have to pivot. I don’t want that for the entire town of Marana.” The Town Council did not heed McGuire’s warnings, nor did they listen to the other people who pleaded that they reject Beale’s proposal. Beale’s promises were enticing: $407 million in tax revenue over the next decade, more than one-third of which would go directly to Marana. A data center, the town’s leaders claimed, would be in Marana’s best interest. The Town Council had in fact passed an ordinance in 2024 restricting data center development. Any facility built in the town would be prohibited from using Marana’s water supply for its cooling systems and would have to adhere to design and noise requirements. Developers would also have to get documentation from the utility provider with proof that there’s sufficient electricity to power a data center. There would be jobs, good ones. Members of various trade unions attended the Town Council meetings and spoke out in support of the data center. Beale employees were present, too, and they brought signs that said “Yes for data centers” to distribute to supporters. No one took them. With the exception of Kai, who recused himself from the proceedings, the council unanimously voted to rezone the land. “I saw more than one person be like, ‘I can’t believe I’m going to have to vote for a liberal with pink hair just to get rid of this stupid fucking data center.’” Marana residents fought back: They collected around 2,800 signatures on petitions asking for a referendum on the data center, only to have the town reject them on a technicality. Residents sued the town, and so did Beale. In the middle of all this, McGuire and three other data center opponents decided to run for Town Council. Their tagline was “Marana for the People.” They held town halls and knocked on hundreds of doors. McGuire, whose politics and presentation are out of step with those of most Marana residents, told me she focused on local policies when talking to voters. “I saw more than one person be like, ‘I can’t believe I’m going to have to vote for a liberal with pink hair just to get rid of this stupid fucking data center,’” McGuire told me. Unlike the other insurgent candidates, she won. The site of the proposed Luckett Road data center in Marana, Arizona. McGuire, now a member of the Town Council, still worries about the long-term effects a data center will have on her community. Beyond the water and power use, she noted that the chips that power data centers have a shorter shelf life than tech companies’ financials would suggest. In other words, the chips themselves will depreciate more quickly than their financial models take into account. Burkart emphasized the tax revenue the project will bring to Marana. He also noted the project’s low water footprint. After construction is complete, the Marana facility will use roughly 6.6 million gallons a year. (After publication, Beale noted that it does not purchase or otherwise procure the microchips in its data centers.) The costs and uncertainties of data center construction are so massive that some major tech companies lack the cash, or the desire, to pay for them outright. McGuire said Beale’s two projects in Arizona would cost a combined $120 billion to build, money that would be funded with private equity and debt, a figure Beale rebuts. According to Burkart, the two projects will cost a combined $8.6 billion. Debt financing isn’t unusual in the tech industry, but the data center buildout requires so much capital that even major financial firms can’t go it alone. Nvidia recently worked with a consortium of six major financial firms that included Blackstone, BlackRock, and Goldman Sachs to finance $500 billion for AI compute; this atypical financing push has been described as more a series of partnerships and memos of understanding than closed deals. For small towns hoping to ride the AI wave, it’s also a risky one. Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Liaquat Ahamed has compared the new AI economy to the railroad boom of the late 19th century, when a handful of companies, armed with generous government contracts, remade the country in their own image and tanked the global economy in the process. The advent of the railroad made Arizona what it is today. It connected the homesteads and ranches scattered throughout the desert to international markets, and to the whims and caprices of global capital. On a blazing Wednesday morning in early August, I stepped out of my air-conditioned car and into the Wild West. There was a miner’s cabin and a sheriff’s office and an abandoned farmhouse, a church, and a saloon where, I understood, gunfights had broken out in the past and would someday break out again. There was a small, inoperable well, an opera house and a carpenter’s studio, a dressmaker, a blacksmith, a bank. There was a ranch complex and an “Oriental Cafe” right next door to the undertaker. Here was a small civilization, an oasis in the inhospitable desert, surrounded on all sides by mountains. Not quite a ghost town, but nonetheless devoid of people. When I walked into the lobby of the Pioneer Living History Museum in north Phoenix, the woman behind the counter asked if I was sure I wanted to be there. Aside from the telephone museum — which I wouldn’t be able to peruse anyway, since the feral peacock that lives on the property had gotten in again, and he was in a foul mood — the whole thing was outside. Outside that day was 105 degrees. The volunteer actors who typically populate the little town weren’t there. Too hot. Well before it became a state, overconsumption of water was encoded into Arizona’s DNA. A paved sidewalk that certainly didn’t exist in the pioneer days led me to the door of a well-appointed Victorian home built in the 1890s for a J. Marion Sears and his family. Though the paint’s yellow exterior now cracks under the intense Arizona sun, it was clear the Searses had lived well. The Sears home, a placard boasted, was one of the first wood-framed homes to be erected in the city. Lumber was hard to come by before the railroad’s tracks reached Phoenix in 1887. Before then all goods had to be freighted into the city, typically by teams of mules, and in fact that was how Sears had made a small fortune. A Confederate veteran, he arrived in the Arizona Territory in 1878 and made a living as a freighter and cattle rancher. Though they lived in the desert, the Sears family homestead was fruitful: Tidy orchards provided them with apples, pears, apricots, figs, and almonds. Image 1 of 4 Scenes from the Pioneer Living History Museum in Phoenix. Scenes from the Pioneer Living History Museum in Phoenix. Scenes from the Pioneer Living History Museum in Phoenix. Scenes from the Pioneer Living History Museum in Phoenix. This bounty was not unusual, but, as detailed in Thomas E. Sheridan’s Arizona: A History , it was precarious. The Sears family, like other white settlers, tended to their crops with water sourced from an intricate network of canals, the first of which was built by the Swilling Irrigation and Canal Company in 1867. Its owner, Jack Swilling, was a hardworking, hard-drinking entrepreneur who often supplemented his whiskey with liquid morphine. He was not, however, a particularly talented engineer, a limitation that ultimately didn’t matter much, because Swilling neither designed nor built the canals that helped white men settle the Salt River Valley. That work had been done centuries ago by the Hohokam, a pre-Columbian people who tapped into the Salt and Gila rivers to build a thriving agricultural civilization in the middle of the desert. By the 16th century the Hohokam had fallen. Their descendants scattered; their canals sat idle and eventually went dry until Swilling thought to revive them. Arizona’s AI boom isn’t something new; rather, it is more of the same, albeit on a grander scale Swilling’s innovation kicked off a new wave of development in Arizona. Homesteaders flocked to the territory, as did speculators who were less interested in eking a living out of the land than getting rich off what lay beneath it. The earth didn’t yield much in the way of precious metals, but it was rich in copper, and it wasn’t long until investors from San Francisco and New York opened up mines and smelters. Across the territory, family farms were crowded out by capital. The cattle conglomerates came first, and with them came alfalfa. Agricultural conglomerates planted wheat and barley and, after some botanical experimentation, tens of thousands of citrus trees, until it all dried up in the national depression of 1893, two years into a drought that drained the canals and the rivers that fed them. After a few parched years Arizona was bailed out by the federal government, which built a reservoir so the people of the Salt River Valley would never again experience privation. Theodore Roosevelt christened his namesake dam in 1911 and predicted that, having harnessed the power of water, the valley would someday be “one of the richest agricultural areas in the world.” Well before it became a state, overconsumption of water was encoded into Arizona’s DNA. Propped up by feats of engineering, Arizona’s economy steadily plugged along until the first World War, when the industrial demands of militarization transformed the desert state into an economic powerhouse. Suddenly there was insatiable demand for everything Arizona produced: citrus and cattle to feed the troops, alfalfa to feed the cattle, cotton for airplane tires, copper for manufacturing. Fortunes grew. “Alfalfa was King,” the Arizona Republican declared in 1917, “Cotton was Queen, and every Dairy Cow was a Princess.” When the war ended and the Depression tanked the economy a decade later, it all went bust again. It took another war to revive the economy. The first indication that things were turning around came in 1939, when a new war in Europe sent metal prices soaring. Even before the United States entered World War II in 1941, the federal government had started looking to Arizona as a training ground for the military, building out flight schools and Air Force bases in the desert. Arizona’s industrial economy is the product of two world wars — and TSMC’s investment in the state is part of a trade war with China, a 21st-century arms race where the end goal is not a nuclear bomb but something critics say is akin to it. Looked at this way, Arizona’s AI boom isn’t something new; rather, it is more of the same, albeit on a grander scale. “It’s crazy to think about where we used to be and what we used to do,” Mackay, Phoenix’s former economic developer, told me. “You’d disappear out into the desert. I could ride my horse to Indian Bend in Pima all the way to the Verde River without seeing a building.” That route now passes three golf courses, a hospital, an indoor water park, an aquarium, and countless subdivisions and strip malls. The Salt River Valley had a population of 11,000 in 1890. Fifty years and several irrigation projects later, just over 65,000 people lived in Phoenix. Last year, the metropolitan area reported a population of more than 5 million. Shockingly, this development isn’t to blame for Arizona’s perilous lack of water. Population growth hasn’t led to an increase in Arizona’s water consumption. Not only does the average Arizonan consume less water today than in the 1980s, but the state’s overall water use has also dropped by 16 percent since then, a decline almost entirely attributable to reduced agricultural demand. But resource conservation can only go so far when the rivers and aquifers that sustain life in the state are drying up , and locals are understandably furious that they’re being asked to reduce their own water consumption while local officials welcome new water-intensive industries. The land immediately surrounding the Pioneer Living History Museum remains largely undeveloped. Here the past remains unchanged and lovingly maintained in honor of the rugged pioneers who made the desert bloom. This is Arizona’s history. And just five miles south, where TSMC’s engineers manufacture the chips that enable the AI industry to reshape life as we know it, lies Arizona’s future. Correction, October 29th: A photo caption has been updated with the correct spelling of Rebecca Chen’s name. Update, October 29th: This story has been updated with statement from Beale.

items.title: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
items.description: Genie 4: our new world model unlocking unprecedented realism in real-time simulation.
items.content: October 27, 2026 Models Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation Raia Hadsell, Diego Rivas and Hang Qi Join the Genie 4 waitlist Your browser does not support the video tag. Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulation’s coherence and continuity. With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences. Your browser does not support the video tag. We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers — gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . Your browser does not support the video tag. Genie 4 delivers enhanced photorealism, fluid movement, and native audio. All accompanying sounds featured above are produced directly by Genie 4. Genie 4 advances four key capabilities The following are recordings of real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves. Shaping world simulation in real-time With Genie 4, you can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene. Between your inputs, Gemini also monitors and steers the scene to keep the world progressing cohesively. Turn on audio to hear Genie 4 worlds. Slide 1 of 3 Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: Use the reference image as the exact first frame and visual basis for the scene. Preserve the same floating rectangular platform, weathered concrete edges, wild grasses, ferns, twisted small tree, warm glowing amber sphere, and the same middle-aged man in a loose brown suit playing a brass saxophone. A cinematic, highly naturalistic documentary scene, photographed on 16mm film with subtle grain, soft photographic detail, extremely low contrast, muted natural colors, lifted shadows, gentle highlights, and soft diffuse overcast light. Absolutely no HDR, no dramatic contrast, no glossy digital rendering, no artificial cinematic lighting. The platform floats in the middle of a vast, quiet lake surrounded by distant misty forests. Thin layers of fog drift above the water. The sky is pale blue-gray and overcast, with a soft, almost monochromatic atmosphere. The warm amber sphere provides a delicate contrasting glow, softly illuminating the surrounding vegetation and reflecting in the lake. Begin with a slightly closer view of the saxophone player than in the reference image, while keeping the platform, glowing sphere, tree, and surrounding lake visible. The man continues playing his saxophone naturally, with subtle breathing, finger movements, and gentle body swaying. The camera moves independently and can freely explore the entire environment, gliding smoothly over the water with gentle, controlled movement. The camera is not attached to the man or the platform. Maintain realistic spatial continuity and natural camera movement. Everything must remain photographic, physically believable, documentary-like, extremely low-contrast, and softly desaturated throughout the entire experience. One continuous shot. Natural lake ambience, distant wind, soft water movement, and realistic saxophone sound. No background music beyond the instruments physically present in the scene. Your browser does not support the video tag. Environment prompt: A wide, sun-drenched hilltop meadow filled with tall green grass and scattered purple, white, and yellow wildflowers swaying in a warm breeze. Low green shrubs dot the right side of the field while distant blue-green rolling hills stretch along the left horizon beneath a bright, partly cloudy sky. Character: Winding in sweeping S-curves through the center of the grassy meadow from the immediate foreground far into the distance is a long, continuous stream of glossy bubblegum-pink satin fabric. The shimmering pink cloth billows, ripples, and lifts softly above the wildflowers like a flowing river of silk as the wind moves beneath its folds. Your browser does not support the video tag. Environment prompt: A sweeping aerial view over the vast, frozen landscape of Antarctica, featuring endless snow-covered glaciers, jagged icy mountain peaks, and sculpted blue icebergs bathed in crisp polar sunlight under a clear, pale blue sky. Numerous hot air balloons dot the horizon at varying altitudes, with a large cream, red, and blue striped balloon floating prominently in the mid-distance above the ice sheet. Character prompt: Shot from a first-person POV standing inside the woven wicker basket of a flying hot air balloon, looking out over the leather-trimmed basket edge on the right side of the frame, where black padded support poles, metal rigging chains, and the dark base of the balloon canopy overhead frame the drifting polar vista. Pushing the frontier in realism for physics and human action Genie 4 introduces a new standard of realism to real-time interactive simulation. Built on an advanced physical understanding of the world, Genie 4 simulates real-world physics scenarios, such as aerodynamics, collisions, and more. The most dramatic leap is how Genie 4 simulates people, creating characters that move naturally, respond organically to their environments, and can be interactively steered in real-time. Slide 1 of 3 Your browser does not support the video tag. Environment prompt: A sunlit outdoor courtyard featuring a weathered stone plinth set against a soft-focus background of lush green garden foliage and clear blue sky, bathed in bright, warm afternoon sunlight that backlights airborne droplets in crisp slow motion. Character prompt: A whole, glossy green-striped watermelon rests in the center of the stone plinth. Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: A macro close up of a maple seed falling from the tree into the grass Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: A crowded rural Japanese train station in the 1980s, packed with passengers waiting along the platform. The only railway inspector in a dark navy uniform stands close to the camera, observing the scene. A long, deep-red local train with many carriages occupies the railway track closest to the camera POV, stretching across the frame and extending far into the distance. The train is clearly visible in the immediate foreground, not on a distant track. People fill the platform naturally, standing, walking, boarding and waiting with luggage. Lush green mountains, cedar forests and humid summer haze surround the station. Authentic 1980s Japanese atmosphere, cinematic 35mm documentary photography, realistic perspective, asymmetrical composition, natural lighting, subtle film grain, photorealistic textures. The station must look genuinely busy, with a dense crowd of visible people throughout the platform. The red train must be on the nearest track, dominating the scene. No empty platforms, no distant train, no sparse crowds, no centered symmetrical composition. Modeling how the world sounds Genie 4 is our first real-time world model to generate audio natively. Every world carries the ambient sound of its own setting, from wind in the trees to waves crashing at the beach. The true frontier, however, is human speech. Genie 4 introduces interactive dialogue that adapts on the fly. Characters converse and react to your inputs or events in the world, all in real-time. Slide 1 of 3 Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: Create a fully three-dimensional immersive stained-glass landscape that feels like a handcrafted crystal window brought to life. The world should be explorable, as if the camera can move freely through a giant 3D stained-glass environment. The entire scene must have a stained-glass / crystal-window look: translucent colored glass, dark lead outlines, glowing layered panels, volumetric depth, and artisanal glass textures. Show a beautiful landscape with a flowing river running through green fields, flowers in the foreground, trees, distant mountains, clouds, and a radiant sun in the sky. The river should feel like flowing translucent blue glass, the flowers like upright stained-glass sculptures, the grass and trees like layered colored-glass forms, the mountains like stacked glass panels, and the sun like a luminous circular stained-glass element. Everything must feel spatial, cohesive, luminous, and handcrafted, with depth and the sensation that the viewer can move through it in three dimensions. The camera should be able to travel through the scene as if walking or gliding inside this 3D stained-glass world. Keep the world beautiful, magical, and fully consistent in style. Absolutely everything must remain made of stained glass or crystal at all times, including the grass, the water, the sky, the clouds, the flowers, the trees, the mountains, the sun, and all visible surfaces. Do not introduce any natural real-world textures. No real grass, no real water, no normal sky, and no realism outside of the stained-glass universe. No text, no modern objects, no realism outside of the stained-glass universe Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: Immersive first-person POV, we only see the big strong hands of the knight rider tightening the reins, dragon and wings. Photorealistic, ultra-realistic action-camera footage seen entirely through the rider's own eyes while riding a gigantic black dragon at 140 km/h through a mountainous dragon-racing course with many dragons and riders. Other dragons are mounted by other knights. The camera IS the rider's eyes. The camera is attached to the rider's head, facing forward, and moves naturally with the rider's head. The rider is the viewer. The rider's face, head, torso, body, and full silhouette are NEVER visible. No third-person shots, no external camera angles, no cutaways, no views of the rider from behind or from the side. Only show what the rider would naturally see: the dragon's neck and occasional parts of its upper back near the bottom edge of the frame, the rushing landscape, two other dragons and their riders racing alongside and ahead, and a huge castle with catapults on its walls. A standard is carried naturally by the rider and may occasionally appear at the edge of the frame, but never blocks the view or fills the frame. The camera maintains this exact first-person perspective throughout the entire flight. Aggressive high-speed racing, powerful realistic wingbeats, aerodynamic weight, intense wind, natural head movement, subtle camera vibration, wide-angle action-camera distortion, realistic motion blur, cinematic natural lighting, physically believable movement. Strict visual constraints: true first-person rider POV, no visible rider, no third-person perspective, no external tracking shot, no drone camera, no over-the-shoulder shot, no cinematic cutaways, no camera floating outside the rider's body, no CGI appearance, no video game look, no 3D-render aesthetic. Audio: deep thunderous wingbeats, roaring high-altitude wind gusts, distant volcanic rumble, and crackling flame embers. Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: A cinematic macro close-up from a 1995 Hong Kong indie romantic drama, shot on 35mm film. Two young, unconventional-looking Korean lovers in their 20s ride a motorcycle across a bridge on the outskirts of Hong Kong at dawn. The male driver wears no helmet, looking around anxiously, while the pale-skinned female passenger wears an open-face helmet. Their faces dominate the foreground, large and overlapping, with natural skin texture and subtle expressions of worry and tenderness. Low-angle panoramic composition, framed by solid black bars. Shallow depth of field, blurred road receding behind them, orange streetlights streaking past, and a dark green dusk sky. Intimate, imperfect, melancholic 35mm film aesthetic. One continuous shot. Simulating complex events with Gemini models Bringing Gemini and Genie 4 together adds a new layer of reasoning to world simulation, allowing us to model complex, multi-step events and test how AI systems navigate different environments before bringing them to the real world. To achieve this in real-time, Gemini 3.8 Flash serves as a guiding agent in the loop: as Genie 4 generates a world in real-time, Gemini continuously observes the scene, breaks down goals into a sequence of steps, and reviews incoming frames to track the progress and verify that each step succeeded. As the world shifts or the user intervenes, Gemini adapts its plan in the moment, unlocking worlds with reliable causality, procedural behaviors, and multi-step reasoning. Slide 1 of 3 Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: Universal Robots UR5 holds a pipette and dispenses liquid into a lab plate, triggering tiny electric sparks. Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: A REAL, ultra-photorealistic, high-end 35mm cinematic first-person perspective (POV) experience set inside an opulent, claustrophobic antique salon, strictly avoiding any video game, CGI, or digital render aesthetic. Real place, cinema, not render. POV & Foreground Wand: Authentic first-person perspective looking down along the player's physical right hand, which firmly grips an ornate, hand-carved hardwood and polished brass wizard wand pointing into the room. The player's skin exhibits realistic pores, skin creases, cuticle texture, and natural muscle tension under ambient room light. The wand displays fine wood grain, tiny varnish micro-cracks, cold metallic brass inlays, and tactile surface wear from handling. Porcelain Menagerie & Room Architecture: A suffocating, baroque-style gallery packed floor-to-ceiling with thousands of fragile, life-sized and miniature glazed porcelain animals. Glistening ceramic peacocks with intricate feather patterns and vibrant cobalt and emerald enamels, regal porcelain dogs, and curled porcelain cats perched on marble mantels, mahogany display shelves, and velvet-draped pedestals. The surfaces showcase authentic high-gloss ceramic glazing, micro-crazing cracks in the enamel, delicate bone china translucency, and natural dust gathering in the crevices. Cinematic Optics & Lighting: Shot on high-end anamorphic 35mm film lenses. Natural optical characteristics featuring shallow depth of field, subtle barrel distortion, realistic optical lens flares, fine organic film grain, and creamy bokeh in the background. Natural daylight streams through tall, grime-streaked Victorian lace curtains, casting soft volumetric dust motes and creating sharp, physically accurate specular highlights across the glossy curved porcelain glazes. Dynamic Movement & Physical Interaction: Continuous, smooth handheld POV traversal. The player subtly sweeps and points the wand toward the ceramic figures, causing realistic micro-vibrations in the frame as footsteps tread across creaking hardwood floorboards. The figures remain frozen in immaculate, fragile stillness, catching shifting highlights as the wand moves. Acoustic Atmosphere: Raw, immersive documentary-grade audio. Faint floorboard creaks underfoot, distant room tone, quiet breathing, the subtle dry friction of fingers adjusting their grip on the wooden wand, and the delicate, crystalline clinking resonance of fine porcelain vibrating faintly in the quiet air. A real magician stands beside a tall wooden table. On the table is a large rectangular wooden box, completely open at the top, with no lid. A real peacock stands calmly inside the box. Exceptional production design, sophisticated art direction, cinematic lighting, natural but carefully controlled light, realistic skin tones, beautiful contrast, subtle shadows, rich textures, elegant composition, shallow depth of field, high-end cinema camera, realistic human actors, extremely photorealistic. It should look like a frame from a prestigious, beautifully shot modern TV series: understated, expensive, cinematic and completely believable. No theater, no stage, no fantasy, no cartoon, no plastic-looking people, no CGI look. Your browser does not support the video tag. Prompt: crowned crane walks across the snow beneath the clear dusk gradient sky. Natural colors in a documentary style. As part of exploring this capability, we have also been experimenting with Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4 to bring our frontier research together with Gemini Robotics . In the example below, Argon breaks down a user-instructed task into steps for Genie to render. These steps are interleaved as text captions to Genie 4 as the simulation is rendering. Because Genie 4 can be steered in real-time with text captions using Gemini, this now unlocks the path of adapting the simulation as it progresses towards the completion of that task. This capability becomes a path for simulating a breadth of scenarios in imagined worlds, using Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4. Your browser does not support the video tag. Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4 work together to simulate Apptronik's Apollo humanoid playing a game of checkers, breaking the task down into real-time steps. Learnings from trusted testers While Genie 4 is a major research milestone, it remains an early, experimental model. To understand how interactive world models can support real-world workflows—and where they still need to grow—we’ve been working with cohorts of trusted testers across creative industries, journalism, education, gaming, and engineering. Testers highlighted how the leap in photorealism, native audio, and real-time steering allows ideas and concepts to be turned into realistic simulations, unlocking new abilities across disciplines: Creative direction : Creatives and technologists are testing Genie 4 as a rapid "draft mode" for pre-visualization and ideation. For example, filmmakers can step into a live simulation of a scene and run multiple "takes" in real-time, adjusting camera angles, lighting, dialogue, and action on the fly. Historical scenarios & immersive photographs : Photojournalists are exploring how a single 2D archival photograph can become a grounded simulation of that environment in seconds. Teams are testing how populated, dynamic worlds can help experience historical spaces or visualize how short-term environmental events, like a flash flood or wildfire, unfold. Interactive experience concept design : Game developers and creative technologists are testing Genie 4 to go from an initial idea to an explorable prototype in seconds, testing visual styles, material aesthetics, and interactive mechanics through natural language prompts before writing a single line of engine code. Simulation : Aside from our robotics research, enterprise partners across industries are evaluating Genie 4 as a tool for rapid "zero-to-one" scenario generation, and identifying gaps to further improve Genie to best fulfill that simulation need. Future work: Towards hybrid world models A promising path for future progress lies in hybrid world models, which combine the logical, structured reasoning of code and language models with the rich, sensory representation of pixel-level simulation. Bringing Genie and Gemini models closer together is an early step in this direction. Gemini works behind the scenes to map the structure and plan the narrative timeline, while Genie generates the immediate physical reality—rendering how the world looks, sounds, and responds, pixel by pixel. Together, these complementary strengths can unlock a new class of world models that are far more coherent, controllable, and grounded than either approach could achieve alone. Building world models responsibly Genie 4 marks a new area of frontier research that merges real-time generation and photorealism, introducing a new range of capabilities and dimensions that we want to roll out and explore in a responsible way. Genie 4 includes strict safety guardrails that are consistent with our safety policies across other models. Before launching this preview, we evaluated Genie 4 through internal rigorous safety evaluations to prevent the generation of harmful or malicious content. Also, we have intentionally deployed it first to trusted tester partners to get early feedback, before we release the model more broadly. To maintain transparency, all video and audio generated by Genie 4 will include SynthID, our imperceptible digital watermarking technology that helps identify AI-generated content across visual and audio modalities. Understanding current limitations Genie 4 remains an early, evolving area of research. While it can maintain coherent environments over short sessions, visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over time—especially as a simulation runs longer, after multiple complex prompt edits, or when navigating throughout the scene. Complex physical interactions, real-time audio accuracy, rendering legible text, spatial accuracy, and long-term consistency are active areas of ongoing research. We are sharing Genie 4 as a preview to learn alongside our community and safely advance the frontier of interactive simulation. Next steps for Genie 4 Genie 4 has been released as a research preview to trusted testers, and is coming soon to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . We’re excited for users to step inside, experiment, and build their own interactive worlds soon. items.title: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction
items.description: Dream is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream's world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
items.content: Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Elder led product design for a team of 800 people building software for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, while Mathur served as a senior vice president in the company’s commercial practice. When the friends decided to build a startup early last year, there was no question they would do it together. Despite having no direct background in architecture, Elder and Mathur were troubled by a growing problem: Fewer buildings are constructed in the U.S. today than a few decades ago , as development costs have surged. “We’ve gone from dial-up internet to superintelligent AI, but our ability to build the physical world around us has actually decreased,” Mathur told TechCrunch. Believing AI can boost productivity across the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, they set out to build Dream , a startup developing built world models that automate building design and engineering. Dream has emerged from stealth with $17 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, alongside other backers, including SV Angel, XYZ, and Zigg Capital. The startup aims to replace cumbersome, outdated AEC tools like Autodesk’s AutoCAD and Revit. If you sit next to an architect or a structural engineer, you’ll notice that they are still “drawing” every piece of their designs part by part on legacy software, Mathur said. “AI really plays no role in that equation.” While a standard LLM like ChatGPT can generate an image of a building, the result won’t be structurally sound. Dream, by contrast, is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream’s world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States. “Our model actually understands what’s within those walls. What materials are used, what the beams are made of, and how much weight they can support,” Elder said. The startup calls its approach “structural cognition” because its model generates structurally precise designs that account for internal building elements like plumbing and HVAC. Dream has already begun selling its product to AEC professionals and developers, who use the model to conceptualize building designs and estimate overall costs, according to the founders. The platform is already deployed across 10 active projects in Texas and California. While Dream isn’t the only company attempting to update AEC software with AI — other startups working on this include Motif , Snaptrude , and Arcol — Elder and Mathur claim that they are the only ones that developed a world model that instantly designs whole buildings. Kimberly Tan, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that while the firm first invested in Dream over a year ago, when the startup model was just an idea, she has been extremely impressed with their progress. “I have not seen anybody take the technical approach,” she said. “They’re doing everything based on their own models.” Topics AI , Andreessen Horowitz , architecture , dream , Palantir , Startups , Venture , world models When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Marina Temkin Reporter, Venture Marina Temkin is a venture capital and startups reporter at TechCrunch. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she wrote about VC for PitchBook and Venture Capital Journal. Earlier in her career, Marina was a financial analyst and earned a CFA charterholder designation. items.title: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 14 +8 Avijit Ghosh evijit Follow hfpolicy Sayeed Choudhury sayeedmd Follow CMU-OSPO Greg Tananbaum gtananbaum Follow ORCA-Open Emma Scharfmann EmmaScharfmann Follow hugging-science Georgia Channing cgeorgiaw Follow hugging-science Eunice Mercado-Lara EuniceML Follow ORCA-Open Irene Solaiman irenesolaiman Follow hfpolicy :last-child]:mb-0"> An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon. Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar , an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University , opens on November 2. See How to Participate below. The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University , Purdue University , Georgia Institute of Technology , Arizona State University , and The George Washington University , all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute ; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA) , through its Fostering Innovation Network , as the community partner. Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org . Making publicly funded science more usable The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development , and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data. But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines. Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI . The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release. The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains , including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models. The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025 , with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader. Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data . When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets . Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X . By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon. This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories. Open Science Challenges Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse. A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit? To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals: Demonstrate scientific reuse. Produce concrete examples of researchers and developers building on publicly funded scientific artifacts, including applications that combine resources across institutions or disciplines. Learn what makes reuse possible. Identify technical barriers, documentation gaps, interoperability challenges, and successful practices that can inform future research infrastructure, funding decisions, and public policy. The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful. The first challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026 The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University , teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios. Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy. Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns. Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available. Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face . How to Join Project ProtoStar Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful. We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org . Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale. items.title: Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
items.description: Accelerating the search for novel antimicrobial peptides using Google Antigravity for Science.
items.content: October 15, 2026 Science Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity Pengfei Tian, Maxwell L. Bileschi, Zoi Tsangalidou, Sukhdeep Singh and Lucy J. Colwell Explore scientific workflows in Google Antigravity New antibiotics are urgently needed to help with rising levels of antimicrobial resistance, but searching for new therapeutics is often a slow, labor-intensive process. With Google Antigravity, our agentic development platform, this process can now be made easier. Google Antigravity provides an agentic science workbench that empowers biologists to discover, structurally evaluate, and prioritize promising targets quickly, compressing what used to be a fragmented search over multiple databases into a single session. It also helps researchers scan through millions of previously uncharacterized proteins in the UniProt database using ProtNLM, a model that predicts biological function from amino acid sequences. This technical walkthrough shows how biologists used Google Antigravity to uncover a novel antimicrobial peptide candidate which has predicted activity against the pathogens involved in respiratory tract infections. The lead identified here is now undergoing wet-lab validation. Finding new antimicrobial peptides Rising antimicrobial resistance is one of the most pressing global health crises of our time and could result in an estimated 10 million annual deaths globally by 2050. To prevent this, we urgently need to discover novel therapeutics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly bacteriocins, offer a promising alternative to traditional antibiotics because they have naturally evolved to target fundamental vulnerabilities in competing bacteria, from cell envelopes to essential intracellular machinery, making it difficult for pathogens to develop resistance. The exponential growth of genomic and metagenomic sequencing has populated global databases with billions of natural amino acid sequences. This pool of natural data has already produced globally used bacteriocins like Nisin, alongside recent genome-mined breakthroughs such as Darobactin, Dynobactin, and Lariocidin. Many, however, remain locked within the unannotated "dark matter" of protein databases, with their function uncharacterized because they aren’t similar to known proteins. For example, the world's leading public resource of protein sequence and functional information, UniProt , holds millions of sequences with unknown functionality, transferred directly from genome sequencing projects. To bridge this gap, Google developed ProtNLM (Protein Natural Language Model) , a deep learning model trained to directly read the underlying evolutionary “grammar” of amino acid sequences. This allows the model to predict biological function directly from raw protein sequences, enriching millions of previously unnamed UniProt entries with high-confidence functional labels. Overview of the ProtNLM pipeline translating raw amino acid sequences into natural-language biological annotations for unreviewed UniProtKB/TrEMBL entries. The functional annotation scope of the system covers protein names, function comments, subcellular locations, and GO terms, in addition to keywords. Collaborative intelligence Scientific discovery is rarely a single step process; finding viable candidate proteins requires human intuition and iteration to incorporate new empirical evidence. Working in Antigravity, the researcher and AI agent begin by setting a focused biological goal: find and computationally validate novel AMPs in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae . During an interactive, multi-turn session the researcher steers the scientific strategy, deciding which questions to ask and what evidence to collect, while the agent handles the heavy lifting of cross-database orchestration, structural analysis, and literature synthesis. Slide 1 of 6 Navigating a vast search space: The agent queries the database and filters millions of entries down to a handful of candidates worthy of attention. Here, the agent finds a bacteriocin (Uniprot ID: A0A0U0D591 ) with a length of 97 amino acids from the Lactococcin 972 family. Validating the novelty of a finding: To verify the novelty of this discovery, the researcher guides the agent to interrogate the candidate against curated knowledge in Swiss-Prot via the EMBL-EBI NCBI-BLAST service and confirm this peptide has no meaningful sequence homolog among manually reviewed proteins. Reasoning over 3D protein structure: The researcher steers the analysis towards structural evidence. The agent retrieves the candidate’s 3D model from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, querying it against experimentally determined structures to identify remote homologs, and superimposing the models to assess similarity. Here, the structural evidence corroborates ProtNLM’s prediction by showing the candidate's fold closely matches an experimentally determined bacteriocin. The structure viewer in Antigravity allows this structural analysis to be seamlessly performed in one place. Reading the biological context around a gene: The agent looks beyond the molecule itself to its genomic neighborhood, reasoning over whether the surrounding machinery supports the AMP hypothesis. Inspecting the flanking genes, it spots a revealing pattern: our previously uncharacterized candidate sits at the upstream of a tightly coupled operon, just 6 base pairs ahead of a ABC transporter permease and its potential partner ATP-binding protein, alongside another annotated bacteriocin and an XRE transcriptional regulator. This provides strong contextual evidence that it is part of a working bacteriocin system. Building a mechanistic hypothesis from the literature : By reviewing the existing literature, the agent proposes how the molecule might act and what pathogens it might act on. In this case, existing evidence suggests a mechanism of action targeting bacterial cell division, and a predicted potency spectrum spanning several drug-resistant pathogens. Generating an experimental plan: Finally, the agent translates its in silico findings into an actionable bench protocol, spanning protein expression, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, target engagement, and in vitro toxicity testing, bridging the gap from computational prediction to wet-lab experiment. This step is already in motion: this candidate - along with several others discovered through the same pipeline - are now in wet-lab validation, where experimental results will provide the ultimate test of the agent's analysis. The candidate we uncover in this walkthrough represents a biologically plausible lead backed by structural and genomic evidence but it still requires wet lab validation. What makes this meaningful is how dramatically it lowers the barrier to everyday biological workflows, turning days of fragmented database triage into a single collaborative session. While this session focused on a narrow amino acid window in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae , researchers can take the conversation in any direction, such as layering in new filtering criteria, exploring different sequence lengths, or targeting other priority pathogens. By broadening the search from human commensals to environmental microbes and beyond, scientists can guide the agent across UniProt to discover novel AMP candidates at scale. A shared 3D canvas for interactive collaboration A protein's 3D structure can help us understand its biological function. Examining a candidate’s predicted fold in space is key. To provide this end-to-end workflow in a single workspace, we are introducing the Biomolecular Structure Viewer , a 3D visualization tool embedded directly into Antigravity. The researcher and agent work together over a shared visual state. As the agent retrieves structures from AlphaFold Database or the scientist’s own predictions, it can dynamically drive the viewer. For instance, it can highlight key functional regions to visually explain its hypotheses. Crucially, this awareness flows both ways: actions like highlighting specific residues or pinning notes directly onto a binding pocket are synchronised back to the agent. A researcher can simply mark a region of interest in 3D space and ask, for example, "How might this β-strand affect Lipid II binding?", allowing the agent to immediately reason over the exact structural context the scientist is looking at. Your browser does not support the video tag. The Biomolecular Structure Viewer inside Antigravity showing the AlphaFold-predicted structure of the candidate bacteriocin, giving the researcher and agent a shared 3D canvas to inspect and annotate functional regions. Accelerating Scientific Discovery Historically, uncovering insights like those in the workflow demonstrated above required fragmented and specialised software: writing custom scripts to query databases, manually exporting files to 3D modelling programs, managing disconnected genomic tools and working with multiple experts to design the wet lab assays. Because wet-lab validation remains resource-intensive, narrowing the search space to only the highest-confidence leads upfront is critical. Using Google Antigravity allows researchers to navigate the vast biological search space efficiently while leveraging accurate protein function predictions from a domain-specific model. Google Antigravity executes this end-to-end scientific reasoning in one place. This allows scientists to spend more time evaluating high-quality hypotheses, running experiments in the lab and solving research challenges. Acknowledgements We would like to acknowledge the contributions of the following team members: Maria Gabriela Cardoso, Victoria Johnston, Lexi Walker, Gena Hong, James King, Richard Green, Filip Radlinski, Artem Sobolev, Michael V. LeVine, Ruijie K. Zhang, Zachary Wu, Luca Schulz, Amy Danson, Tristan Oliver Kwan, Ryan Krueger, Oleg Kovalevskiy, Doug Fritz, Yunhan Xu, Sebastian Nowozin. Special thanks to Stephanie Lo from EMBL-EBI for her valuable feedback. Explore scientific workflows in Google Antigravity
