items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta Published October 15, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 75 +69 Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow merve merve Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Guarin Flück guarin Follow Quentin Gallouédec qgallouedec Follow Alvaro Bartolome alvarobartt Follow Serveurperso Serveurperso Follow Jun Kim Jundot Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input. Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date. Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here . Overall Capabilities and Architecture Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images. Feature Muse Spark Open Model size ~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token Expert routing 256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token Inputs Text, images, audio, and video Output Text Context window Up to 1M tokens Checkpoint formats BF16 and NVFP4 The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4. Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each. Mixture of Experts The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum. Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp , vLLM, and SGLang recipes below. Perception Encoder A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention. Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images. Audio Encoder Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm. Long Context The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text. Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context. Inference Support Transformers The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template. Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed. You can initialize the model and processor as follows. import os from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoTokenizer, DistributedConfig distributed_config = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B " ) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" , distributed_config=distributed_config, ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Explain in one sentence why the sky is usually blue." }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, reasoning_effort= "medium" , # default: xhigh, options: low/medium/high/xhigh add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) Text-only Inference Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template , enabling add_generation_prompt=True , tokenize=True , return_dict=True , and return_tensors="pt" . Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt. messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "high" , # options:low/medium/high/xhigh ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) generated_tokens = output[ 0 ][inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.decode(generated_tokens, skip_special_tokens= False )) Images and Text The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt. image_url = ( "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/" "resolve/main/pills.jpg" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : image_url, }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?" , }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize= True , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_effort= "medium" , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) response = processor.decode(outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], skip_special_tokens= False ) processor.parse_response(response) Video Inference Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor: processor.video_processor.fps = 4.0 As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template . Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate. import torch messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "text" , "text" : ( "Describe what happens in this video. " "Use timestamps and include relevant speech or sounds." ), }, { "type" : "video" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vlm_test_images/resolve/main/ramen.mp4" }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_from_video= True , return_metadata= True , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 256 , do_sample= False , ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] response = processor.batch_decode( generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True , )[ 0 ] print (response) Audio Inference The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference. If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood: import torch from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id). eval () messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "audio" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/audio-samples/resolve/bbaudio_question_39.mp3" , }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Answer the question." , }, ], } ] # Downloads the audio, decodes it as mono, resamples it to 24 kHz, pads it, creates input_values_mask, and expands the audio placeholders. inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_backend= "auto" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , ) # Decode only newly generated tokens prompt_length = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] generated_text = processor.batch_decode( output_ids[:, prompt_length:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) print (generated_text[ 0 ]) The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings. Tool Calling Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows. from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM MODEL_ID = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" # Load model processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) tools = [ { "type" : "function" , "function" : { "name" : "weather.get" , "description" : "Get the current weather for a city." , "parameters" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "city" : { "type" : "string" }, }, "required" : [ "city" ], }, }, } ] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/SF.png" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "I'm going to the city in this picture. What clothes should I wear?" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_strength= "high" ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs) response = processor.parse_response( completion, prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools, ) print (response) Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below: <|begin_of_text|> <|start|>system<|message|> You are a helpful AI assistant. Knowledge cutoff: 2026-01-04. Current date: ... ... <|eot|> <|start|>user<|message|>... <|eot|> <|start|>assistant <|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason, to=self<|message|>the model reasons here<|eom|> # reasoning <|start|>assistant to=user<|message|>final answer<|eot|> # final answer self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response. Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template : <|start|>assistant to=weather.get<|message|> <atem:function_calls> <atem:invoke name="weather.get"> <atem:parameter name="city">San Francisco</atem:parameter> </atem:invoke> </atem:function_calls> <|eot|> Llama.cpp Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command: curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF:Q2_K The repository containing quants is here . Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model). You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more. ## Text-only inference curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ] }' ## Image-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"What is in this image?"}, {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' ## Audio-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"Transcribe this audio."}, {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":"data:audio/wav;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K . SGLang The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs. From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" SGLANG_FLASHINFER_NVFP4_PER_TOKEN_ACTIVATION=1 \ uv run sglang_meta serve \ --model-path "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --quantization modelopt_fp4 \ --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \ --tp-size 4 \ --ep-size 4 \ --port 30000 The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API: curl http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content . vLLM The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs. After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 \ VLLM_PLUGINS=musespark1x_models,ptq_nvfp4 \ vllm serve "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --tokenizer-mode musespark1x \ --config-format auto \ --load-format internal_safetensor \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \ --reasoning-parser musespark1x \ --tool-call-parser musespark1x \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --port 8000 This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request using the same Hub model ID: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' MLX Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit , ready to use right away. We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer. Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks. The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this: mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \ --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \ --max-tokens 5000 This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details. Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead. To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint. The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses . curl "https://<your-endpoint>.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/pills.jpg"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?"} ] }], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} }' Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key. Fine-tuning with TRL You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer . This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples . First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig , which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads: from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig distributed_config = DistributedConfig(fsdp_size= 64 , ep_size= 8 ) In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch. Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case. import torch from datasets import load_dataset from peft import LoraConfig from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer train_dataset = load_dataset( "allenai/tulu-3-sft-mixture" , split= "train[:500000]" ) training_args = SFTConfig( output_dir= "muse-spark-lora-sft" , model_init_kwargs={ "dtype" : torch.bfloat16, "distributed_config" : DistributedConfig(fsdp_size= 64 , ep_size= 8 )}, per_device_train_batch_size= 1 , max_steps= 500 , max_length= 2048 , packing= True , save_only_model= True , logging_steps= 1 , report_to= "trackio" , ) trainer = SFTTrainer( model= "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" , args=training_args, train_dataset=train_dataset, peft_config=LoraConfig(r= 16 , lora_alpha= 32 , target_modules=[ "q_proj" , "k_proj" , "v_proj" , "o_proj" ]), ) trainer.train() The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen. Then we can run this command across each node: torchrun --nnodes 8 --nproc_per_node 8 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint " $MASTER_IP :29700" sft_muse_spark_open.py We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run. Demos Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork. 3D Asset Generator We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js . You can find the prompt here , as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra. We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process. Browser Interactions with OpenEnv and Hugging Face Sandbox We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here . Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components: Muse Spark Open served with Inference Endpoints, OpenEnv wrapping web driver actions with helium and selenium (click, type, scroll etc) defining browser environment’s reset, step, observation, termination interface, Chromium web browser where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below. You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo. Call your Browser Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon. Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria. Wrapping Up Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants . If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions. items.title: Putting Earth AI to work: Geospatial agents for our planet's biggest challenges
items.description: Earth AI
items.content: Putting Earth AI to work: Geospatial agents for our planet's biggest challenges October 14, 2026 Shravya Shetty, Distinguished Engineer, and Luke Barrington, Product Director, Google Research In a new technical report, we demonstrate how combining domain-specific foundation models, spatial tools, and upfront planning enables a Geospatial Reasoning agent to carry out complex spatial analysis and planetary prediction that standalone LLMs can’t. Following promising tests with partners, we’re also expanding experimental agent access via Ask Google Earth and an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) service. Quick links Microsite Technical report Interest form Research@ top 10 News from Google collection page Share When we introduced Google Earth AI , we shared a suite of geospatial foundation models — spanning remote sensing, weather, flood hydrology, and population dynamics — alongside an initial prototype showing how a Gemini-powered agent could connect those models to answer cross-modal questions. Since then, we have evolved a Geospatial Reasoning agent from an early concept into a much more capable, experimental system built for multi-step, geospatial reasoning across planet-scale data and autonomous training of custom predictive models. Today, we are sharing three updates: A new technical report on geospatial reasoning: We present systematic evaluations across four benchmarks, including GeoKTools and GeoExpertQueries, two new benchmarks we developed and are releasing for researchers to test their own geospatial reasoning agents. Our results quantify the value of Earth AI’s specialized tools and planning over out-of-the-box LLMs. Insights from real-world partner testing: Over the past few months, we invited a small group of social impact and commercial partner organizations — including the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa , People in Need , GiveDirectly , the Milken Institute and WPP — to test the agent in support of their own real-world workflows, such as disease outbreak investigations, disaster preparedness, and clean energy screening. Expanding early access on Google Earth and Google Cloud: We are expanding experimental access for both multi-step geospatial analysis and for planetary prediction. We’re offering early access to an experimental deep research update for Ask Google Earth . We’re also providing early access to an agent-to-agent API for developers building custom workflows, including integration recipes for connecting to Gemini . What’s new in Geospatial Reasoning General-purpose LLMs and standard coding tools struggle with real-world spatial problems because planetary datasets are massive, with specialized map and satellite formats that require careful multi-step planning to combine accurately. To tackle complex spatial workflows in practice, our agent brings together four key capabilities: Connected to Earth AI foundation models and planet-scale data The agent connects Gemini to the capabilities of Earth AI’s foundation models — including WeatherNext , Flood Forecasting , the Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) , AlphaEarth Foundations and Remote Sensing Foundations — alongside information from Google Maps Platform (e.g., place information, routing, air quality, rooftop solar potential), Google Earth Engine , Data Commons and Google Dataset Search . Modular skills, upfront planning and a dedicated spatial workspace Earth AI capabilities are packaged as modular skills that the agent calls only when a user question needs them. Before running complex operations, the agent builds a step-by-step analytical plan, selects appropriate fallback datasets when local coverage is sparse, and processes large map layers in a dedicated workspace. This approach avoids overwhelming the agent context with massive amounts of spatial data, while preserving accuracy and tracking data attribution. Every response shows the agent’s plan and the data sources used so experts can check assumptions or substitute datasets. Bring your own data Organizations rarely rely on public data alone. Users can now input their own datasets via the Geospatial Reasoning agent API as CSV spreadsheets, custom map boundaries ( GeoJSON ), or cloud tables. Users can then ask the agent to join their private locations with Earth AI’s global models and catalogs. From multi-step reasoning to autonomous Planetary Prediction Beyond answering complex analytical questions, the agent also powers our recently announced Planetary Prediction Engine . Given a user’s local outcome data, such as regional disease rates, crop yields, or grid outages, the agent automatically selects relevant population and environmental signals, uses our Population Dynamics Insights and the annual Satellite Embedding dataset (Google products built on PDFM and AlphaEarth Foundations , respectively) and trains validated machine learning models for spatial prediction, super-resolution downscaling, and forecasting. In our recent public health research , combining these population and satellite signals improved predictions of health outcomes by 12% over demographic baselines and enabled mapping at 8X finer spatial resolution. Our Geospatial Reasoning agent responds to a user’s question by first planning a multistep workflow, then selecting key Earth AI tools, datasets and models that are relevant to the query, and finally executing each stage of the plan in a workspace outside the context window. The answer incorporates multiple Earth AI capabilities into a text, tabular and map-based report. Evaluating a Geospatial Reasoning agent To measure the impact of domain-specific tools and upfront planning on geospatial reasoning, our technical report compares four agent configurations across Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro: (1) a standalone LLM, (2) the LLM with basic web search and maps grounding tools, (3) the LLM with Earth AI tools (such as Remote Sensing Foundations and WeatherNext 3) but without upfront planning, and (4) the full Geospatial Reasoning agent which begins every query with a dedicated planning stage that reasons over available capabilities to assess what it can and cannot do and sets out the stages of retrieval and processing needed to reach an answer. We evaluate four agent configurations, from the base Gemini model, to agents progressively augmented with skills and orchestration that are optimized for geospatial reasoning. The evaluation spans four benchmarks, covering expert-level open-ended analysis, multi-tool orchestration, and community-developed geospatial problems with deterministic answers. CBGB and UnivEARTH are two externally developed benchmarks that test geospatial code generation and question answering respectively. To test agents on challenging tasks that go beyond a single question or use case, we developed two new benchmarks. GeoExpertQueries introduces complex, real-world queries with expert-authored golden workflows that capture analysis best practices in domains like crisis resilience, site selection and public health. GeoKTools contains templated queries with verifiable answers, each requiring correct selection and use of 1 to 4 distinct geospatial tools. Together, this suite provides substantially broader coverage than prior evaluations of geospatial reasoning systems. To accelerate research and development of geospatial agents, we release the development splits of both our new benchmarks in full. Example queries from our new GeoKTools ( left ) and GeoExpertQueries ( right ) benchmarks. GeoKTools tests an agent’s ability to select and use specific geospatial tools and datasets while GeoExpertQueries evaluates reasoning on open-ended, multi-step workflows. Results and key takeaways Two key takeaways stand out from our evaluation: First, domain-specific skills are essential for spatial reasoning. The agent with only basic tools (web search, maps grounding and code execution) struggles on quantitative spatial tasks. Equipping the agent with Earth AI skills drives a significant jump across GeoExpertQueries, GeoKTools, and CBGB. The only exception is UnivEARTH, where even a standalone LLM scores 93.6%, likely because the source NASA articles and answers are available on the public web. Second, upfront planning unlocks open-ended, real-world workflows. While Earth AI skills alone are enough for narrower tasks like those in CBGB and GeoKTools, tackling open-ended problems in GeoExpertQueries requires upfront planning to keep the agent on track across multi-step analyses and prevent it from making unreliable assumptions or taking shortcuts like using web-search instead of spatial tools. The table below shows scores across all four benchmarks using Gemini 3.8 Flash: Scores are 0–100, averaged over three runs. Each benchmark is scored differently, so compare within a row, not across rows. The technical report also discusses limitations. GeoExpertQueries scores come from an autorater that compares the agent’s performance to expert workflows that define the steps an analysis should take, not the correct final answer. We therefore consider the agent’s output as a strong first draft for experts to review and build on, not a final answer. Earth AI in action: Early testing with partners To evaluate how this research translates to real-world challenges, we gave a small group of partners early access to test the experimental agent on their toughest problems. Across public health, disaster response, and infrastructure planning, below is an overview of how they are putting Earth AI into action: World Health Organization (WHO AFRO) & DRC’s INRB : At the start of the 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), WHO AFRO’s Emergency Preparedness and Response Hub in Dakar used the Geospatial Reasoning agent to map remote mining corridors where the exposure risk and human mobility are high by cross-referencing forest loss (from satellite images), mining sites (from maps and web data), and population data. In minutes, the team pinpointed 48 exposed settlements and located more than 45,500 at-risk people — a process that normally would have taken weeks. This allowed local responders to proactively deploy mobile laboratories and coordinate border surveillance. Meanwhile, the Epidemic Modeling and Intelligence Unit (UMIE) at the DRC’s National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB) used the Planetary Prediction Engine to estimate the risk of Ebola spreading into uninfected zones. By combining mobility flows with historical case trends and Earth AI models and datasets, these weekly insights give coordinators critical planning time before cases arrive. “Mobile populations like miners move faster than traditional paper surveillance can track, creating dangerous blind spots. Earth AI fills those gaps with satellite and mobility signals—moving us from reactively chasing a virus to actively forecasting where it will strike next.” Dr Etien Koua , HIS Program Area Manager & Hub Coordinator for WHO AFRO Emergency Preparedness and Response ( watch the video ) People in Need : Geospatial reasoning helped combine natural disaster forecasts with population and imagery information, shifting analysts’ focus from data processing to providing insights: "The experimental Geospatial Reasoning agent helped us analyze 14 historical cyclone paths to identify high-exposure villages in minutes rather than days of manual GIS work, turning prepared complex data into immediate insights and freeing up critical time for life-saving anticipatory action." - Alonso Gonzales , GIS and Remote Sensing Coordinator GiveDirectly : Teams uploaded custom map boundaries to rapidly calculate population exposure by wind-speed zones during Tropical Cyclone Maila and benchmark tornado damage in Mississippi, cutting crisis scoping from days to minutes inside a single workspace. WPP : Used geospatial reasoning to connect Population Dynamics Insights with their proprietary data. Their case study demonstrates how Earth AI insights enhanced the performance of geospatial marketing campaigns, while preserving the privacy of their data. Milken Institute : Pre-development teams used the agent to combine their own lists of 1,500+ candidate buildings with Google Maps Platform’s Solar API and census data in order to screen locations for building community resilience hubs, taking into account rooftop solar potential, mobility data, nearby transit hubs, climate risks, and federal investment zone eligibility. Watch the film Link to Youtube Video Early testing with these partners helped our evaluation and expansion of the agent’s geospatial skills, driving our recent additions of road-network routing, support for larger user-uploaded datasets, and better discovery of authoritative local data sources. Expanding early access: Where you apply to test it Today, we are expanding access across our Earth AI research capabilities to gather more feedback on these experimental geospatial reasoning capabilities. We are making these available to a limited group of early users: Ask Google Earth : preview expanded deep analysis capabilities directly inside Ask Google Earth. This provides an interactive chat experience where you can ask complex spatial questions in natural language, analyze data — including your own — in Google Earth projects, and explore visual results directly on the map. Geospatial Reasoning Agent API : For developer teams that want a customizable, do-it-yourself integration to power custom workflows, we offer an experimental headless Agent-to-Agent(A2A) service. Early partners can connect the Geospatial Reasoning agent to their own custom agents and data pipelines. We provide step-by-step developer recipes for teams who want to connect the service to their Gemini for business environment. Our Planetary Prediction Engine capabilities are also available for early preview — accessible both through an interactive interface for rapid, plain-language modeling and via the Agent API for custom workflows. To express interest in getting access to these research capabilities, please complete our interest form . To be among the first to try out our early stage projects, you can also sign up for our Early Access Pool . items.title: Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review
items.description: General Science
items.content: Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review October 14, 2026 Rajesh Jayaram and Vincent Cohen-Addad, Research Scientists, Google Research Following successful deployments across 16,000+ submissions at STOC, ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR, Deep Review is launching publicly. It’s expanding from deep mathematical and scientific peer review to provide rigorous, grounded verification across knowledge documents, including Google Docs and presentations. Quick links Paper STOC 2026 Blog Post ICML 2026 Retrospective NeurIPS 2026 Blog Post Google Labs Portal R@ Top 10 Blog News from Google R@ Collection Page Share Generative AI has accelerated many technical fields. It is now common for AI to play some role in writing scientific papers and technical documents, running code, designing experiments, and drafting proposals. However, accelerating content creation has created a review challenge: the human capacity for verification has remained largely fixed amid this rapid increase in AI-generated content. Reviewing complex documents like long scientific manuscripts or complex legal agreements requires specialized expertise and advanced subject knowledge. This imbalance creates a validation bottleneck , where information is being generated faster than it can be rigorously reviewed. Today, we’re excited to announce the public release of Deep Review , an agentic AI system engineered to provide rigorous feedback and technical verification on complex documents. Initially designed for computer science academic paper analysis, the system’s capabilities have expanded to review documents across many domains, such as legal and finance. It can be used as both an iterative improvement tool during the drafting process and a tool for the scientific process verification, claims, and evaluation during the review process. Deep Review represents the evolution of our Paper Assistant Tool (PAT) — an experimental initiative developed to help researchers stress-test manuscripts prior to conference submission. Over the past year, we partnered with four flagship computer science conferences ( STOC 2026 , ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027 ) to provide private, pre-submission feedback to authors of more than 16,000 manuscripts who opted in. Further details on PAT and these pilots can be found in our manuscript, Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google’s Paper Assistant Tool . With this release, Deep Review is now accessible worldwide: Tiered access and scalable API : Every user receives two complimentary document reviews per week. Users with high-volume workflows can connect their Gemini API key for higher usage limits and programmatic integration via the Deep Review API. Format flexibility : Deep Review will initially support PDFs and plain text as input formats, with support for multi-file inputs coming soon. Privacy and data policy : Documents uploaded to Deep Review are never used to train, fine-tune, or improve Google models. Uploaded documents are stored for one year for the sole purpose of display to the user in the Deep Review UI. Deep Review accelerates technical validation One of the most significant examples of the validation bottleneck is in academic peer review. This can be seen in the uptick of submissions to academic publication venues, especially venues for AI research itself, which have seen a dramatic rise. This year, there were over 74,000 submissions to three major AI conferences ( ICLR , NeurIPS , and ICML ) up from approximately 45,000 in 2025, 32,000 in 2024, and 23,000 in 2023. Each of these submissions requires multiple high-quality reviews to ensure the integrity of the peer review process, which can place a larger burden on human experts. Increase in submissions to NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR between 2023 and 2026. Deep Review aims to help alleviate this expanding burden on human reviewers across technical fields. By providing detailed, objective evaluations of documents, Deep Review checks logical consistency and mathematical statements, suggests improvements, grounds facts, and compares with existing work. It addresses some of the most cognitively burdensome facets of review, while leaving higher-level judgements to humans. A proven track record for scientific review Deep Review has been extensively tested and deployed under its experimental name, the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), in four pilot partnerships with the flagship computer science conferences STOC 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027. During these pilots, authors were able to opt-in to receive feedback and analysis on their paper via PAT in the weeks before the submission deadline. The goal was to provide authors with actionable feedback to help improve the quality of papers in submission. This feedback was completely decoupled from the official conference review process. PAT did not collect any of the data for training, and papers were deleted from Google systems promptly after each program concluded. Author reactions to the tool have been extremely positive, and reflect continued improvements to both underlying models and the PAT harness. With the addition of Gemini 4 Argon support in Deep Review, the underlying capabilities of the tool have further increased beyond the older iterations of PAT described below. Statistics and author feedback from the pilot programs of PAT at machine learning and theoretical computer science conferences. How Deep Review works Single-prompt LLM calls often fail when evaluating long, complex documents due to exhausting their token reasoning budget, overlooking long-context cross-section dependencies, or accepting nuanced claims without fully scrutinizing them. Deep Review solves these challenges through a four-stage agentic pipeline: Document segmentation : The document is first ingested and autonomously decomposed by a segmenter agent into logical segments (e.g., Introduction, experiments, methodology, etc.). These segments can be overlapping, and must cover all the content of the input document. Adaptive budgeting : Not all sections require equal cognitive depth. The pipeline inspects information density and dynamically allocates a compute budget, along with a specialized inference scaling pipeline for each section. For instance, sections with dense mathematical proofs may receive more compute than an introduction or a related work section in an academic paper. Deep parallel verification : Specialized reasoning agents scrutinize each segment in parallel. Each agent has access to the full document context to track cross-references, but focuses its reasoning power specifically on the task of reviewing its specific target section. This ensures both that reviewing tasks are manageable for each review swarm, and that parallel swarms are properly coordinated. Global synthesis and agentic grounding : A dedicated synthesis agent consolidates the segment-level reports, and does final consistency checks between sections, rerunning logical checks if required. The agent further performs external grounding checks and tool calls as a final preventative measure against hallucinations. System architecture showing the four-stage pipeline. Universal verification and review: Beyond research papers While Deep Review originated in academic paper reviews, long-context review is generalizable: reasoning mechanisms used to check whether a mathematical proof holds up in a research paper can also help surface logical gaps and inconsistencies in other types of documents, where claims must be backed by evidence. Therefore, Deep Review can be used to bring structured critique to a broader range of everyday workflows. Users can now apply Deep Review to analyze complex documents across many domains. For instance, it can be run on: Design documents: Catch unstated architectural assumptions, spot edge cases, and suggest concrete improvements. Presentations: Ensure slide transitions flow logically and bulleted takeaways match visual charts. Legal and financial documents: Check internal consistency across clauses and data tables, flag ambiguous terms or downstream consequences, and ground claims against supporting evidence. Deep Review meets Antigravity We’re also introducing the Teamwork Deep Document Review Pattern , a document review implementation pattern inspired by Deep Review built into Antigravity using the Teamwork multi-agent orchestration framework . This pattern is designed systematically to evaluate research papers, manuscript drafts, and technical proposals using a multi-agent hierarchy with self-correction and segment-based rubrics. Antigravity users can invoke this pattern using the /teamwork-preview command. Making thorough, high-quality technical reviews widely accessible Comprehensive pre-submission critique in computer science has generally depended on access to extensive review networks — like senior faculty, well-resourced academic laboratories, or extensive peer advisory networks. Providing reliable, automated logical verification can help many academics stress-test their assertions, identify avoidable flaws, refine and strengthen their documents based on verified foundations, and present their work in a review process with more confidence. Get started We invite researchers, engineers, and creators everywhere to explore Deep Review: Try Deep Review: Visit the Google Research Portal to review your first documents. Integrate with the API: Access programmatic verification in your continuous integration and drafting workflows using your Gemini API key . Read the research: Read the preprint to explore the underlying methodology and pilot evaluations. Conclusion and looking ahead Given the utility it demonstrated during our pilot programs with academic conferences, we believe that tools like Deep Review will play a significant role across the peer review process in the coming years by empowering both authors and reviewers. Moving forward, we are continuing to expand the platform’s capabilities. With the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon support, Deep Review’s underlying capabilities further improve, delivering even higher quality feedback and analysis to authors. Additionally, with multi-file support coming soon, users will also be able to run these same consistency checks across entire sets of related documents, spreadsheets, and exhibits simultaneously. We hope these advancements will make high-quality technical reviews more widely accessible for knowledge workers everywhere. Acknowledgments Deep Review is a collaborative effort across Google Research, Google DeepMind, and Google Cloud. We thank our core contributors and research collaborators — Santiago Balseiro, Taylan Cemgil, Tommaso D'Orsi, Kirk Draheim, Lindi Emoungu, Ayse Erduran, Palash Goyal, Caroline Hartnell, Shobana Kannan, Amy Keeling, Siyi Kou, Bridget Lee, Ian Li, Anoushka Mazumdar, Taylor Montgomery, Mouad Naciri, Uche Okonkwo, Mihir Parmar, Anthony Phalen, Rory Pilgrim, Sarah Presotto Post, Rob Tierney, Drew Tyler, Vishnu V., Vahab Mirrokni, Laura Vardoulakis, Johannes Welbl, David Woodruff, Yunhan Xu, Jinsung Yoon — as well as our executive sponsors Katherine Chou, Corinna Cortes, Burak Gokturk, Vahab Mirrokni, Tomas Pfister, Yossi Matias and the Program Chairs of STOC, ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR for their partnership. items.description: General Science
items.content: play silent looping video pause silent looping video unmute video mute video Research@ 2026: 10 ways we're amplifying human ingenuity October 14, 2026 Yossi Matias, Vice President, Google & GM, Google Research Update • oct 20, 2026 Since the initial release of this post, Synaptics launched the Synaptics Astra SR200 Series Edge AI chip, built using our co-designed open-source Coral NPU. Today, at our flagship Research@ event, we're sharing research breakthroughs that amplify human ingenuity. From planetary intelligence to advanced medical workflows, we’re putting capabilities once out of reach in the hands of people worldwide. Here are 10 highlights. Quick links Earth AI for public health News from Google collection Earth AI technical report Deep Review blog Share We are living through a golden age of research and scientific discovery. For the scientists and researchers at Google Research, the opportunity extends beyond pioneering breakthroughs. We’re also building and sharing robust tools that empower the global ecosystem. AI acts as an amplifier of human ingenuity, creating the conditions for curiosity and rigorous inquiry to flourish. Today, at our Research@ event in Mountain View, we are demonstrating how we put never-before-possible insights and capabilities into the hands of doctors, scientists, developers, public health officials, and others. Here are 10 highlights: 1. Google Earth AI enables planetary intelligence for organizations and society Addressing global challenges requires accurate, real-world planetary intelligence. With Google Earth AI , it becomes possible to forecast public health threats , accelerate clean energy investments, provide businesses with foresight, and more. Today, we’re expanding early access and inviting partners to explore three new ways to access Google Earth AI’s new, experimental capabilities : Conducting deeper geospatial analysis as part of an early access experimental feature in Google Earth . Generating risk assessments and forecasting different scenarios via our planetary prediction engine . Integrating our Geospatial Reasoning agent skills directly into custom workflows via an experimental agent-to-agent API, provides developers with programmatic access to core features like satellite imagery parsing, routing and demographic embeddings. We’re also announcing the integration of Google Dataset Search for querying from more than 100 million public datasets, and TimesFM for planetary nowcasting and forecasting iterations. All these capabilities are powered by over 70 geospatial tools including planetary foundation models like Remote Sensing Foundation Model (RSFM) and Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM). They are validated by empirical benchmarks detailed in today’s Earth AI Technical Report . They enable developers, health leaders and enterprise teams to automate complex geospatial workflows. To further support social impact efforts, Google.org is providing $10 million in funding to organizations working on crisis resilience and public health. This includes $2 million to The Milken Institute to unlock infrastructure bottlenecks for affordable housing, clean energy, broadband, safe water systems, and other essential infrastructure. Google Earth AI ’s geospatial foundation models are being used to help predict disease outbreaks and enable public health teams to take proactive, preventive action. 2. Multi-agent orchestration helps scientists build on existing knowledge Existing literature offers a great source of knowledge for driving new scientific discoveries. We built a multi-agent orchestrator, enabling scientists to reproduce previous methods and analyses and then apply them in new settings to tackle important research challenges. As an example, this helped researchers apply a new methodology for solving inverse design problems in fluid mechanics to the design of urinary catheters. They discovered catheter designs that, in simulation, were better at preventing bacterial infections. This complements our existing tools to accelerate scientific workflows. Empirical Research Assistance enables scientists to generate and test thousands of code variations in parallel, and has helped researchers produce results from biology to cosmology to economics. Co-Scientist , built in collaboration with Google DeepMind, is a multi-agent tool that can generate novel hypotheses and has already helped partners, like researchers at Stanford University, uncover repurposed medicines to fight liver fibrosis. 3. Deep Review helps authors improve the clarity and accuracy of technical documents Thorough peer review is a core part of the scientific method. We created Deep Review , an agentic system that provides rigorous verification across complex documents. This is particularly important as AI is increasingly being used to help experts draft technical documents. Many Google researchers and external authors have already used an early version of this system to review over 16,000 research publications submitted to top-tier computer science conferences. It helps with the heavy cognitive lifting by checking logical consistency and grounding facts, while scientists maintain authority over creative direction. Today, we’re expanding access to Deep Review to the general public to help people verify a variety of technical documents from legal agreements to financial reports. System architecture showing the four-stage pipeline. 4. Next-gen Edge AI chip enables manufacturers to build the wearables of tomorrow With the rise of wearable devices, hardware manufacturers need the tools to develop efficient edge applications to meet the high expectations of customers for all-day performance. Earlier this year, we launched the first Coralboard from Synaptics , using Google’s Coral NPU accelerator core. It enables AI and ML engineers to rapidly prototype and build devices. On October 20th, Synaptics launched the Synaptics Astra SR200 Series , their next-gen, low power Edge AI chip, which includes our co-designed open source Coral NPU. The chip delivers greater efficiency and performance for design engineers building the next generation of smart glasses and watches, connected cameras, streamers, and industrial vision and voice systems. The new low-power Edge AI chip from Synaptics, as displayed next to a coin for its relative size. 5. TimesFM and TabFM transform how businesses work with numbers While language models excel with text, business and operational decisions also rely on numbers. TimesFM and TabFM are foundational models engineered specifically to reason over raw numerical distributions — time-series streams (data that changes over time) and structured tabular data (like spreadsheets). Both models deliver accurate predictions out of the box with zero training. They rank at the top of leading public benchmarks in their fields and are available to all Cloud BigQuery users. Today, we are announcing our upcoming integration of these models into Gemini for business . Soon, business owners, analysts, operation leads or coordinators can forecast trends like product sales or hospital bed capacity, based on complex operational tables and millions of rows of data. Sensitive data stays safely within an organization’s perimeter, and people get the answers they need in seconds. TimesFM-3's multivariate forecast helps to anticipate sales lift for a business on planned promotion days in the future. 6. MedGemma enables innovators to build and deploy health AI applications MedGemma , published last week in Nature Medicine , has been downloaded more than 10 million times by more than 65,000 unique innovators. It serves as an open foundation for developers building specialized applications . Developers have adapted it to meet the needs of their local communities, from enabling faster triage in overcrowded clinics to screening for eye disease and cervical cancer . As developers fine-tune MedGemma for more specialities and care settings, we’re pushing the frontier of open health AI. Our latest research advances MedGemma with tool use, so it can draw on available health records and other applications clinicians rely on. We’re exploring new modalities like mammography, ultrasound and electrocardiograms. Early signs point to substantial gains in capabilities, such as answering clinical questions and interpreting radiology scans, skin images and pathology slides. With these advances, we hope to expand what innovators can build, bringing effective healthcare to more communities around the world. Watch the film Link to Youtube Video 7. AMIE study advances the frontier of how conversational AI can support patients and clinicians With our research on AMIE , we’re exploring the use of AI in clinical reasoning and conversations, to understand how it could empower clinicians and strengthen the patient-clinician relationship. Our research this year in Nature advanced AMIE’s capabilities beyond initial diagnosis toward long-term disease management, and in Nature Medicine , we showed how it can reason across multimodal data like medical images and lab results. Our new study in The Lancet offers a promising look into how its capabilities could come to life in real-world clinical settings. At Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center , 98 patients safely consulted AMIE ahead of urgent care visits, and clinicians reported that the AI summaries helped them prepare in 75% of cases. We’re also advancing AMIE’s multimodal capabilities towards real-time video consultations and have embarked on a nationwide randomized study of AI in real-world virtual care settings in partnership with Included Health . AMIE is part of a rigorous research journey going back to our landmark MedPalm paper, and it’s still early days. Watch the film Link to Youtube Video 8. Groundsource makes it possible for researchers to predict natural disasters AI can help us predict disasters with greater accuracy and lead time, giving communities a better chance to prepare and save lives. We’ve been making progress towards our crisis resilience north star : a world where no one is surprised by a natural disaster. Take flood forecasting . Our global hydrologic model , published in Nature , allows us to provide reliable river forecasts up to 7 days in advance covering more than 2 billion people in over 150 countries for the most significant and impactful riverine floods. Yet just one year ago, predicting flash floods still seemed out of reach. Groundsource is our recent AI-powered methodology that turns publicly available information about crises into high-quality historical datasets, allowing researchers to build more accurate predictive models. We first applied Groundsource with Gemini to analyze flood-related news reports and created a structured dataset with over 2.6 million flood events. This dataset helped us overcome a lack of ground-truth data for flash floods and train a new model that can predict the likelihood of flash flooding in urban areas up to 24 hours in advance. The dataset is now part of the Google Earth AI collection and we've made it openly available to help scientists conduct further analysis and research. A global map showing the density of flood events in Groundsource. Red dots indicate floods from GDACS. 9. Learning interactives give teachers the ability to create custom, guided simulations With generative UI, we can go beyond static outputs to dynamically generate functional, interactive software. Our research experiment explores this in the domain of education. We fine-tune generative UI with pedagogical guardrails to enable teachers to create custom, guided STEM simulations tailored to their curriculum. The sample library features over 30 AI-generated learning interactives, all vetted by teachers, for middle and high school physics, chemistry, biology, and math. Schools can sign up to the Google for Education Pilot Program to share feedback. This will help us improve the simulations and develop more for public use, making practice far more interactive and engaging. play silent looping video pause silent looping video unmute video mute video 10. Play with Putty facilitates collaborative, real-time prototyping for teams Play with Putty allows teams to build and prototype together in a shared environment without breaking their creative flow. It demonstrates what’s possible as AI models become more efficient and capable of generating entire interfaces from natural language prompts. People can interact directly with any part of the interface, while multi-player editing supports seamless, real-time collaboration. We first designed Play with Putty to empower our researchers and teams across Google to prototype together — for example, exploring new solutions and visualizations with Google Earth AI. We’ve since opened up the waitlist on Google Labs to bring the joy of human collaboration to teams using AI everywhere. These 10 updates highlight recent progress from our extensive research portfolio across many domains . Technology succeeds when we amplify human ingenuity. In this golden age of research and scientific discovery, the opportunity is greater than ever — to pioneer breakthroughs and share tools that empower others, in collaboration with many. We’re excited about the journey ahead. items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B Team Article Published October 13, 2026 Upvote 74 +68 Raahul Vignesh Raahul26 Follow LiquidAI Song Duong sduong Follow LiquidAI Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare akhileshdeepakgotmare Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Jiahui Wang WWWjiahui Follow LiquidAI Mayank Agarwal mayankagarwal Follow LiquidAI nathan ranchin nathanrchn Follow LiquidAI Sergei Tilga tilgasergey Follow LiquidAI Sinoué GAD GAD-cell Follow LiquidAI Tim Seyde tseyde Follow LiquidAI Zetian Li zetianli Follow LiquidAI changyi yang changyiyang Follow LiquidAI Simon Lee yungisimon Follow LiquidAI Leonie Monigatti iamleonie Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Karthik Macherla karthikrmacherla Follow LiquidAI Alfred Eng alfredeng Follow LiquidAI Khoi Nguyen KTLK Follow LiquidAI Paul Pak paulpak58 Follow LiquidAI xx tugot17 Follow LiquidAI Tarek Dakhran tdakhran Follow LiquidAI Anthony Maltsev amaltsev Follow LiquidAI Aldo Gael Carranza agcarranza Follow LiquidAI Tyler Murray undfined Follow LiquidAI Aditya Tadimeti adityatadimeti Follow LiquidAI Jimmy T.H. Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI :last-child]:mb-0"> LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware. Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19. Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap. Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) Teacher specialization Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks. MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks. Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Benchmark results We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters. Benchmark LFM2.5-24B-A2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B) AutomationBench 27.69 8.72 5.46 2.61 BFCLv4 65.01 65.00 57.09 53.78 ToolSandbox 80.71 75.02 72.09 75.13 LiveClaw 48.09 38.19 41.25 37.72 PinchBench 83.18 89.93 77.12 84.20 τ³-Bench Banking 8.04 7.63 4.54 7.01 WebArena Verified 26.75 37.62 25.62 28.69 GPQA Diamond 74.42 83.69 74.90 72.42 AA-Omniscience -24.90 -24.35 -59.39 -3.58 HLE 7.40 7.69 8.57 5.65 IFEval 96.75 93.06 92.00 94.19 IFBench 74.69 64.21 47.44 71.67 Multi-IF 84.38 81.53 82.19 82.34 MATH-500 96.04 96.73 95.66 96.40 SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) 51.00 66.20 25.80 53.40 SciCode 32.71 37.35 35.42 27.78 *All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters. For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads. These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. Inference speed on CPU and GPU LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX. Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory. GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300. How to use LFM2.5-24B-A2B Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0 ): pip install -U transformers Then load and run the model: from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map= "auto" , dtype= "bfloat16" , # attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" <- uncomment on compatible GPU ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt= True , skip_special_tokens= True ) prompt = "What is C. elegans?" input_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : prompt}], add_generation_prompt= True , return_tensors= "pt" , tokenize= True , )[ "input_ids" ].to(model.device) output = model.generate( input_ids, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.05 , max_new_tokens= 512 , streamer=streamer, ) Use it in your agent harness Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent: hermes config set model.provider custom hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1 hermes config set model.default LFM2.5-24B-A2B hermes config set model.context_length 131072 hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080 , vLLM uses 8000 , SGLang uses 30000 , and LM Studio uses 1234 . See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples. Get Started with LFM2.5-24B-A2B Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today: Download: LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base and LFM2.5-24B-A2B on Hugging Face. Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi. Fine-tune: adapt LFM2.5-24B-A2B to your task with our fine-tuning tutorials . We can't wait to see what you build.
