items.fingerprint: pairing industrial ai autonomy and human control|technologyreview.com/2026/10
items.title: Pairing industrial AI autonomy and human control
items.content: Industrial intelligence Pairing industrial AI autonomy and human control Living digital twins are helping industrial plants run more like living systems, and setting the stage for industries that work in sync. Most people associate industrial environments with cold steel and clockwork machinery. Functionally, though, a plant or factory is more like a living thing: It has a pulse, even a metabolism. It goes through wear and tear as it ages, and signs of deteriorating health often show up as barely perceptible irregularities. Digital twin technology has long aimed to mirror that dynamism and model anomalies that may be symptomatic of larger problems. But earlier implementations were a few beats behind physical reality; they were incapable of real-time analysis and unable to proactively address any issues detected. They focused more on simulation, observation and what-if scenario planning, rather than closed-loop execution. Rather than serving as a digital mirror of reality that can spot anomalies or suggest optimizations, a living digital twin combines a dynamic, high-fidelity digital representation of complex operations with the capacity to intervene in the physical world through operations and control systems. AI is at the center of this change. Rob McGreevy, chief product officer at AVEVA, likens newer, AI-infused digital twins to organisms that grow and evolve. These “living” versions are adaptive, evergreen models of a plant’s assets and processes. Because they keep pace with live conditions and connect systems that once ran in isolation, they provide a previously missing layer of visibility and orchestration that better reflects the organic rhythms of the facility itself. Now, agentic AI is also enabling industrial systems to move beyond diagnostics or suggestions and act of their own accord. As the technology progresses toward greater autonomy, it’s starting to develop the reflexes for a kind of industrial homeostasis, in which small, constant adjustments keep a plant or factory healthy and humming. All that said, human judgment and operator oversight still play an instrumental role by defining what healthy looks like to begin with—and flagging when AI systems are falling out of alignment. Living digital twins provide the means for human engineers to monitor what AI is doing and ensure execution is on track. The technologies that keep digital twins in sync Living digital twins link engineering and design information with real-time operational data through a digital thread, or a connected record of an asset that follows it through its lifecycle. A couple of notable technological shifts have helped string this thread together: Sensors (which have gotten more affordable in recent years) now stream telemetry from IoT devices and industrial control equipment, and software platforms bring that information into user-friendly interfaces. Predictive and physics-based models can also provide AI-enriched insights into how a machine or process might behave. “You can look at the digital twin through the lens of sustainability: What are my emissions? Or, through the lens of maintenance: Is this asset performing in a healthy way? Or, through a performance metric: Is it producing the number of widgets I need?” Rob McGreevy, Chief Product Officer, AVEVA The lenses through which operators view digital twins have evolved in turn. “You can look at the digital twin through the lens of sustainability: What are my emissions?” says McGreevy. “Or, through the lens of maintenance: Is this asset performing in a healthy way? Or, through a performance metric: Is it producing the number of widgets I need?” Setting boundaries for semi-autonomous systems The next phase is letting AI act on select insights those lenses illuminate. For their part, manufacturers are eager for this chapter: In a 2026 Manufacturing Leadership Council survey of manufacturers (opens in new tab) , 66% said they are using or plan to use agentic AI in their operations, and 40% expect some degree of factory autonomy by 2030. At the same time, they’re wary of the potential risks: In Deloitte’s 2025 smart manufacturing survey (opens in new tab) , 65% of executives ranked operational risk, including the potential for business disruption, among their top concerns. Manufacturers are accelerating toward agentic AI and greater factory autonomy 0 % 66 % of manufacturers say they are using or plan to use agentic AI in their operations 0 % 40 % of manufacturers expect some degree of factory autonomy by 2030 Source: MIT Technology Review Insights with data from Manufacturing Leadership Council (opens in new tab) , 2026 “There is a lot more refinement to be done, a lot more proof points, testing, and validation needed,” McGreevy says about the ongoing process of making AI autonomous. In the near term, McGreevy expects agentic AI to follow the path seen in other industrial technologies like SCADA systems. “The ‘S’ in SCADA means supervisory, and supervisory means there’s a human in the middle,” he says. He sees AI working mostly in that advisory mode for the foreseeable future, with full autonomy limited to narrow, highly repetitive tasks. As for the role human operators play, the day-to-day is evolving. Workers who once specialized in a single process line or maintenance task can now take on multiple disciplines. They can spend less time and effort approving routine actions one by one, and more on defining acceptable operating limits. Because AI can reinforce patterns in the data it receives, catching missteps early is a core part of the job. Human knowledge and experience in interpreting what AI is seeing and doing is instrumental. Governance on a company- and industry-wide scale, too, needs to adapt to the times. Organizations must establish clear guardrails for which decisions AI can make on its own and how its actions are monitored and audited. Still, many have yet to set up comprehensive safeguards: In a recent study from AVEVA and IMD (opens in new tab) , 43% of organizations said AI has changed decision-making and accountability across ecosystem partners only slightly or not at all, while just 23% reported a significant or fundamental change. (Only 27% reported sharing data substantially or extensively with partners.) In the meantime, regulators are starting to define some of the rules. The EU AI Act classifies certain AI safety components used in critical infrastructure as high-risk and imposes requirements for human oversight. Companies are setting up their own structures as well; AVEVA, for one, has a responsible AI governance board and a published set of principles for how AI is developed and deployed. Agentic AI and living digital twins: Real-world case studies Inside the semi-autonomous systems already running, that oversight looks different from one deployment to another. In some cases, an operator approves every action; in others, AI acts on its own while people oversee and define the boundaries it can operate within. McGreevy cites several examples of what machine autonomy and human-plus-machine collaboration looks like among AVEVA customers: At Saudi Aramco’s Yanbu refinery, optimization algorithms adjust production in a closed loop, with operators overseeing as needed. At its Ras Tanura refinery, the algorithms recommend changes, and operators decide whether to implement them. Nestlé uses AI optimization at Nesquik plants to tune the industrial dryers used to produce powdered beverage ingredients. In a landmark test, this tuning reduced energy use by 16%, while improving quality and yield. At Thailand’s SCG Chemicals, an AI-supported digital twin spanning engineering, operations, and maintenance monitors asset health and flags potential failures. The company reports 99% plant reliability and a ninefold return on investment within six months. The National Laboratory of the Rockies in the U.S. has built a generative AI model for grid control rooms to provide oversight at scale. The model supports operators with renewable energy forecasting and estimates of grid conditions. Looking to the future The same synchronization that was once missing from individual plants’ technology systems has also been lacking on a larger scale. “Manufacturing and critical infrastructure have operated as siloed systems for the last 50 years,” says McGreevy. But certain emerging technologies, he suggests, are creating opportunities for more holistic coordination. On an enterprise level, this might involve the integration of physical AI: systems that pair robotics and sensing technologies with AI-powered decision-making. Drones that fly over pipelines and power lines, for instance, can feed visual inspection data to algorithms that spot gas leaks and other hazards. Not only does this create a more accurate and interconnected flow of information, but it spares humans from needing to physically enter potentially dangerous environments. “The robotics-meets-software convergence will mean fewer incidents, fewer outages, and a more sustainable way of operating,” McGreevy predicts. “The robotics-meets-software convergence will mean fewer incidents, fewer outages, and a more sustainable way of operating.” Rob McGreevy, Chief Product Officer, AVEVA A bigger-picture version extends beyond any one plant or process to entire industrial networks, something McGreevy dubs the “integrated value chain.” “Living digital twins make digital manifestations of the entire value chain possible,” he says. “This allows companies to react quickly to supply chain changes, demand changes, tariffs, and material availability.” Amid today’s realities of turbulent geopolitics and shifting regulatory demands, such resilience will be “an absolute necessity,” adds McGreevy. “Without it, it will be very hard to run an effective business.”

ai.summary: Industrial intelligence Pairing industrial AI autonomy and human control Living digital twins are helping industrial plants run more like living systems, and setting the stage for industries that work in sync.
keyTakeaways: Most people associate industrial environments with cold steel and clockwork machinery.
Functionally, though, a plant or factory is more like a living thing: It has a pulse, even a metabolism.
It goes through wear and tear as it ages, and signs of deteriorating health often show up as barely perceptible irregularities.

items.title: Empowering frontline maternal care with AI-assisted ultrasound
items.description: Health & Bioscience
items.content: Empowering frontline maternal care with AI-assisted ultrasound October 21, 2026 Angelica Willis, Research Engineer, Google Research, and Nichole Young-Lin, Clinical Lead, Google for Health A prospective multi-center study demonstrates how AI-based blind sweep ultrasound assessment can enable non-sonographer operators with low-cost probes to deliver expert-level gestational age assessments, marking a significant step toward expanding life-saving maternal care globally. Quick links Paper Share The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that more than 250,000 preventable deaths occur worldwide each year due to pregnancy-related complications. While prenatal ultrasound can improve outcomes and reduce fetal and maternal mortality, two-thirds of people globally lack access to diagnostic medical imaging like ultrasound. Current methods that support maternal health rely heavily on specialized clinical training, leaving millions in low-resource settings without access to a single ultrasound during their entire pregnancy. We saw an opportunity to conduct research towards addressing this real-world need, by developing machine learning systems that interpret " blind sweep " ultrasounds. This way of scanning allows frontline healthcare workers without specialized sonography training to perform scans by simply gliding low-cost, portable ultrasound probes across the abdomen in a standardized pattern. play silent looping video pause silent looping video unmute video mute video Blind sweep sequence protocol diagram in order of their appearance in the data collection protocol. Because many regions face critical shortages of experts, and traditional sonographer training is both expensive and requires a multi-year commitment, enabling these health workers to perform assessments with minimal training has the potential to significantly expand prenatal screening coverage. Combining the minimal training requirement with AI interpretations could ultimately mean a successfully developed tool that has the potential to increase availability of ultrasound-based pregnancy assessment, and thereby improve access to higher quality maternal health. In “ Generalization of AI-Based Gestational Age Assessment Using Blind Sweep Ultrasonography ”, published in JAMA Network Open , we evaluated how effectively an AI model for gestational age assessment (how far along the pregnancy is) generalizes across diverse clinical settings and hardware. While our previous research validated the model's performance on unseen patients from the same retrospective cohort it learned from, this new prospective study shows how the AI system performs reliably running live on mobile devices in real clinics, with only novice operators and unfamiliar ultrasound equipment, and minimal fine-tuning. “ The gestational age is basically how far along a woman is in pregnancy. All of our screening, a lot of our treatments, a lot of our indications for delivery are all based on this master timeline that you get from the gestational age .” - Nichole Young-Lin, OB-GYN Physician Evaluating performance across diverse clinical settings For a medical AI system to safely scale globally, it must demonstrate generalizability — maintaining accurate diagnostic performance when introduced to new clinical settings with different patient populations, clinical workflows, and ultrasound hardware variations than those on which the model was trained. In this study, our original AI model was minimally tuned on only one of our target populations, and then prospectively tested across both target environments: Northwestern Medicine : An urban, high-resource academic medical center in Chicago, IL, United States. Jacaranda Health: An urban community clinic network in Nairobi, Kenya. Originally trained on ultrasound data collected in North Carolina and Zambia using a set of Sonosite, GE, and Butterfly Networks commercial ultrasound probes, the research AI system was paired with Clarius C3, a commercial handheld transabdominal probe. All of these sites differed in various care dimensions, including when women first come in for prenatal care, how many routine ultrasounds they receive, and how gestational age is usually dated. To evaluate efficient system tuning, the study leveraged a small pilot dataset of 120 participants from Chicago — approximately 6% of the original training set—to adapt the model to new probe hardware and extend the gestational age prediction range beyond 36 weeks. To understand generalizability, no data from the Nairobi site was used for fine-tuning, maintaining the Kenyan clinical validation as a strictly independent, external test. To evaluate comprehensive utility, the study also included multiple gestation pregnancies, which could present tracking and measurement challenges for both human operators and automated systems. Our blind sweep model, trained on 1,968 participants (North Carolina, US, and Zambia) was fine-tuned on scans from 120 participants from Chicago, Illinois. It was then tested prospectively in Chicago (n=192) and Nairobi (n=193), with no fine-tuning on Nairobi data. The model was non-inferior to expert sonographers at determining gestational age, in both settings, with a combined mean absolute error of 4.18 vs. 4.48 days. Key findings: Matching the expert standard We compared the AI system’s ability to estimate fetal age from blind sweep ultrasounds to formula-based estimation from the clinically standard expert approach. This expert approach relies on an expert sonographer locating multiple specific cross-sections of the fetus(es) to take precise biometry measurements, a difficult-to-scale task that requires years of training and is highly operator-dependent. Evaluating a primary cohort of 385 participants between 16 and 36 weeks of pregnancy, the diagnostic study demonstrated strong AI system results: Clinically non-inferior accuracy : Across both cohorts, the AI model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 4.18 days in estimating gestational age, successfully demonstrating non-inferiority to the standard clinical procedure performed by expert sonographers, which had an MAE of 4.48 days. Cross-setting generalization : In Chicago, the adapted model achieved an MAE of 4.10 days. In Nairobi, with zero local optimization, the model achieved a comparable MAE of 4.27 days. The AI system's gestational age error (MAE 4.18 days) was non-inferior to expert sonographer biometry (4.48 days), and stayed consistent from Chicago (4.10 days) to Nairobi (4.27 days), where the model had no local fine-tuning. Beyond accuracy, exploratory metrics showed that the research AI system was resilient in complex scenarios. For instance, in cases of fetal weight extremes (above the 90th percentile), the model outperformed traditional biometry formulas, demonstrating robustness against variations in fetal size. Lessons learned during prospective deployment In addition to highlighting an immense opportunity to expand ultrasound access through AI, the prospective multi-center study allowed us to actively observe and optimize how AI behaves in live clinical environments. By deploying our system directly into everyday clinical workflows, we gained practical insights that help us design for real world use. For example, we observed the importance of swappable batteries over plug-in docking stations for keeping devices charged between consecutive patients. These studies also demonstrated how deploying AI systems like this will also require building deep trust with both clinicians and patients. One important way to ultimately achieve this would be by building clear safeguards into the app, like model confidence estimates produced by our model to reject poor-quality sweeps and convey model uncertainty to the clinician user. Looking ahead: Expanding access to care with AI These study findings indicate that AI-based systems can analyze standardized “blind sweeps” images acquired by operators without specialized sonography training. The AI estimate of fetal age had accuracy comparable to the current standard of care from expert operators and more expensive traditional, cart-based ultrasound machines. Demonstrating technical generalizability across diverse clinical settings, hardware, and changing populations, marks a key step in highlighting their potential to expand access to this critical capability for maternal health. By empowering minimally trained community health workers to perform reliable ultrasonography assessments, this research demonstrates the potential to expand prenatal coverage for millions in under-resourced areas. Studying the capabilities of this scalable technology lays the groundwork for more resilient, accessible healthcare systems, ensuring that every mother, regardless of location, has the chance for a healthy pregnancy and a safe delivery. This point-of-care research represents a potential application of our broader vision for expanding healthcare accessibility through AI. The insights gained from this research inform the development of our next-generation, multimodal medical intelligence research. Through our continued work, we strive to provide the development community and scientists with the answers they need to improve clinical care and make it helpful and accessible to all. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-authors across Google Research, Jacaranda Health and Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine: Chace Lee, Justin Krogue, Anneka Wickramanayake, Stacey Caron, Priscah Cheruiyot, Amber Watters, Alicia Martín, Tiya Tiyasirichokchai, Akib Uddin, Yun Liu, Patricia Strachan, Sunny Jansen, Alyssa Santi, Preeti Singh, Catherine Arguelles, Kenneth Hudson, David Melnick, Mahesh Vaidyanathan, Mozziyar Etemadi, Yossi Matias, Avinatan Hassidim, Greg Corrado, Shruthi Prabhakara, Daniel Golden, Ryan G. Gomes, and Shravya Shetty. Thank you to Pi-Chuan Chang and Dale Webster for reviewing this work. items.title: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 51 +45 Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow Régis Pierrard regisss Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla , or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU , a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu" , and you're done. Wait, what's a TPU? 🤔 TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit . TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini. TPUs are available on Google Cloud , from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale. The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in. The old way Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA ( torch_xla ). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about. To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers. Enter TorchTPU 🚀 TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command: pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch . Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU. Your favourite libraries, now on TPU Transformers Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu" . That's it. from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map= "tpu" , # will load model directly on the TPU ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) inputs = tokenizer( "The future of AI is" , return_tensors= "pt" ).to( "tpu" ) out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 64 ) print (tokenizer.decode(out[ 0 ], skip_special_tokens= True )) The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup. Images? Videos? Diffusers paints them on TPUs 🎨 TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu") . For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain. import torch from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium" , dtype=torch.bfloat16 ) pipe.to( "tpu" ) # eager mode: that's the whole change # optional: compiled mode pipe.transformer. compile (backend= "tpu" , fullgraph= True , dynamic= False ) image = pipe( "a corgi astronaut planting a flag on a pizza moon" ).images[ 0 ] The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph. Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe. Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4: TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1 MiniMax-H3 (video + audio) Qwen-Image-2.1 "The fluffy plush Hugging Face mascot from the picture, a round yellow smiling face with rosy cheeks and two little open hands, stands at the prow of an ancient Greek trireme […] Sound of crashing waves, creaking timber, wind in the rigging, distant seagulls, and a low epic orchestral swell." · 1344×768, 5.2 s, 49 steps · 188 s compiled, 262 s eager "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, reading a book by candlelight, oil painting" · 1024×1024, 40 steps · 3.5 s compiled, 8.0 s eager "A neon shop sign that reads 'QWEN IMAGE 2.1', rainy night, reflections on wet pavement" · 2048×2048, 40 steps Kernels The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost. TPU kernels are written in Pallas , which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model: from kernels import get_kernel from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu" kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version= 1 , trust_remote_code=[repo_id]) ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register( "tokamax_ragged_dot" , kernel.experts_forward) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507" , experts_implementation= "tokamax_ragged_dot" , ) The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B. Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation. We test it so you don't have to 🧪 We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[ https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard] . The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress! It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream. If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do. Get started TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu" . TorchTPU on GitHub TPU kernels on the Hub Cloud TPU documentation We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it. More Articles from our Blog partnerships gcp spaces Google Cloud TPUs made available to Hugging Face users 24 July 9, 2024 partnerships gcp hardware Making thousands of open LLMs bloom in the Vertex AI Model Garden 22 April 10, 2024 Community Edit Preview Upload images, audio, and videos by dragging in the text input, pasting, or clicking here . Tap or paste here to upload images Comment · Sign up or log in to comment Upvote 51 +39

items.fingerprint: mps in pytorch 2 15|huggingface.co/blog/mps-pytorch-2-15
items.title: MPS in PyTorch 2.15
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> MPS in PyTorch 2.15 Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 34 +28 Irakli Salia Isalia20 Follow Khushi Agrawal khushi-411 Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads. A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors. TL;DR FP8 comes to the Mac: store float8_e4m3fn values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU! MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing. Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster. More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition. Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB. More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing. Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later ; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later . A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding. What this means for you If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice: Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with torch.compile , Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. ( More ) Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. ( More ) Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows ( reported in ComfyUI ). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB. FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and F.scaled_mm multiplies them directly on the GPU. ( More ) Contents Getting started FP8 comes to MPS Faster language-model decoding Linear algebra gets a boost Convolutions, padding, and training Softmax and reductions A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding More control with MPS streams More operations work on MPS A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16 Wrapping up Getting started You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix ). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why. To try the release candidate in a separate environment: uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu FP8 comes to MPS FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16. You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm , which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor: import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def quantize_fp8 ( x ): limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn). max scale = x. abs ().amax().clamp_min( 1e-12 ) / limit return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale x = torch.randn( 1 , 1024 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.float32) weight = torch.randn( 1024 , 1024 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.float32) x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x) w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight) y = F.scaled_mm( x_fp8, w_fp8.t(), scale_a=x_scale, scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise, scale_b=w_scale, scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise, output_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) print (y.shape, y.dtype) Faster language-model decoding Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers. Linear layers MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear , so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup . The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×. Mixture-of-experts layers A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation . In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well. For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16: import torch import torch.nn.functional as F tokens = torch.randn( 64 , 64 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.bfloat16) weights = torch.randn( 3 , 128 , 64 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.bfloat16) ends = torch.tensor([ 16 , 48 , 64 ], device= "mps" , dtype=torch.int32) out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(- 2 , - 1 ), offs=ends) print (out.shape) # torch.Size([64, 128]) The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile , MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second : Linear algebra gets a boost Complex-valued computations Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization , LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU: import torch a = torch.randn( 8 , 8 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64) a = a + 8 * torch.eye( 8 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64) b = torch.randn( 8 , 2 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64) lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a) x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b) print ((a @ x - b). abs (). max ().item()) Small matrices and larger solves Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates , and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication. Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides. SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values , very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True , which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable. Convolutions, padding, and training Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal: Operation What changes in 2.15 conv1d forward Specialized kernels replace MPSGraph, plus an im2col-plus-matmul path for short outputs. Useful for audio and streaming-model shapes. Constant padding Moves to Metal kernels, fixing runaway driver-memory growth in tiled video VAE decoding (more below). Reflection and replication padding New Metal implementations that are faster and fix backward correctness. Out-of-place dropout nn.Dropout and F.dropout now use the existing fused kernel. Upsampling backward A Metal gather kernel replaces the MPSGraph resize-gradient path. Channels-last conv2d backward Stays on an efficient channels-last path instead of an NCHW graph with costly strided access. Softmax and reductions Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs , about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes: A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB : Memory metric MPSGraph padding Metal padding Current tensor-allocation peak 4.422 GiB 4.095 GiB Allocator-reserved peak 8.070 GiB 8.070 GiB Total driver-memory peak 270.135 GiB 8.108 GiB More control with MPS streams You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream. Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result: import torch x = torch.randn( 1024 , device= "mps" ) torch.mps.synchronize() worker = torch.mps.Stream() with torch.mps.stream(worker): y = x.square() x.record_stream(worker) del x worker.synchronize() print (y.cpu().shape) More operations work on MPS Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp , torch.logspace , torch.take and Tensor.put_ , torch.heaviside , torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons . logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element. Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly . A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16 Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release. Faster LLM decoding Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels , so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context: Model Before After Change LFM2.5-8B-A1B 108.8 tokens/s 126.0 tokens/s +16% Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 52.9 tokens/s 62.8 tokens/s +19% Qwen3.8-27B 12.1 tokens/s 12.6 tokens/s +4% Attention runs entirely on Metal Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely : every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms. More MPSGraph to Metal migrations The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond. A smaller install Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default , with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication. Wrapping up PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try! What's next for us More MPS: 2.16 will run attention entirely on Metal, and we'll keep moving operations off MPSGraph. torch.compile : we're working on getting rid of graph breaks, so more models compile end to end. Your ideas: what else should we work on in PyTorch? If something is slow, missing or broken, on MPS or anywhere else, open an issue on GitHub and let us know. A big thank you to Nikita Shulga , Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release. items.title: Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers: The latest open image generation model from Black Forest Labs Published October 15, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 50 +44 Aritra Roy Gosthipaty ariG23498 Follow Sayak Paul sayakpaul Follow Linoy Tsaban linoyts Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control . You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move. Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection : Checkpoint What it is Defaults black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein Time step distilled, for fast inference 16 steps, no CFG black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base Base model 50 steps, CFG You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now! TL;DR One model for text-to-image, multi-reference image-to-image, and bounding-box layout control. The distilled checkpoint makes a 1024 × 1024 image in about 2 seconds on an H100. NVFP4 and FP8 weights load with from_single_file , for smaller GPUs. LoRA training scripts for both text-to-image and image editing. Ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline, so you can pop blocks out or add your own. Contents Getting started What FLUX.3 can do Base model and quantized variants LoRA finetuning What it costs to run The architecture Modular Diffusers Try it Getting started Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder): pip install -U diffusers transformers Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image: import torch from diffusers import ModularPipeline pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained( "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein" ) pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) pipe.to( "cuda" ) pipe(prompt= "a red fox" , output= "images" )[ 0 ].save( "fox.png" ) What FLUX.3 can do Text-to-image FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height , width , or num_inference_steps to change them. prompt = ( "A wide-angle wildlife photograph of a red fox standing alert in a snow-covered forest clearing at golden hour. " "The fox is centered in the frame, its thick orange winter coat contrasting with the fresh white snow, breath " "visible in the cold air. Snow-laden pine trees fill the softly blurred background, and low warm sunlight rakes " "across the scene from the left, casting long blue shadows." ) fox = pipe( prompt=prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] fox.save( "fox.png" ) Text to image Image-to-image Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want , with the change included. prompt = ( "The same red fox in the same snow-covered forest clearing, now at night under a full moon: cool blue " "moonlight, deep shadows, stars visible through the pine branches, the fox's eyes catching the light." ) night = pipe( prompt=prompt, image=fox, # from the previous text to image example generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" , )[ 0 ] night.save( "night.png" ) Image to image With several references, refer to them in the prompt as <ref_image_0> , <ref_image_1> , ... in the order they are passed to image : red_fox = pipe(prompt= "a red fox" , generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] bench = pipe(prompt= "a wooden bench" , generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] combined = pipe( prompt= "The fox from <ref_image_0> sitting on the wooden bench from <ref_image_1> in a snowy setting." , image=[red_fox, bench], output= "images" , )[ 0 ] combined.save( "combined.png" ) <ref_image_0> : a red fox <ref_image_1> : a wooden bench The fox on the bench Layout control Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id , a bbox , and a desc , and the caption mentions it as <id> . Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max] , y first , on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size. Placing regions in a new image layout_prompt = ( "Minimalist graphic illustration featuring a black silhouette of a person <silhouette_1> centered against a " "solid, vibrant chartreuse background <background_1>. The figure is captured in a dynamic, mid-stride running " "pose, facing toward the left side of the frame. " '[{"id": "background_1", "bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "desc": "A flat field of neon yellow-green with a subtle ' 'paper texture and fine, organic grain."}, {"id": "silhouette_1", "bbox": [150, 150, 850, 850], "desc": "A ' "black silhouette of a person in motion, made of dense stippled ink. The leading edges are solid; the trailing " 'arm and leg dissolve into coarse square pixels and scattered dots."}]' ) runner = pipe(prompt=layout_prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] Each region's desc is drawn inside its bbox Moving regions within a reference image For edits, each region says where its content comes from ( src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes ( tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is. This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire: from diffusers.utils import load_image knight_image = load_image( "knight_orig.png" ) edit_prompt = ( "In <ref_image_0>, move the miniature grey amigurumi knight figure <knight_1> upwards and to the left along the " "yarn cliff <cliff_1>. Keep the rest of the image completely unchanged, preserving the blurred yarn backdrop " "<backdrop_1>, the large knitted dragon <dragon_1>, and the fiery orange thread <fire_1>. " '[{"id": "knight_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [500, 150, 850, 350], "tgt_bbox": [194, 55, 544, 255], ' '"desc": "A miniature amigurumi knight crocheted from thick grey woolen yarn."}, ' '{"id": "backdrop_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], ' '"desc": "A soft, out-of-focus backdrop of cream and indigo knitted yarn."}, ' '{"id": "cliff_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], "tgt_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], ' '"desc": "A steep cliff of stacked yarn skeins in mustard, terracotta, and indigo."}, ' '{"id": "needle_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], "tgt_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], ' '"desc": "An oversized polished steel tapestry needle."}, ' '{"id": "dragon_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], ' '"desc": "A large, fluffy knitted dragon in terracotta and mustard yarn."}, ' '{"id": "fire_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], "tgt_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], ' '"desc": "Curled puffs of fiery orange angora thread suspended in mid-air."}]' ) moved = pipe(prompt=edit_prompt, image=knight_image, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] The knight moves from its src_bbox to its tgt_bbox , and the rest of the scene stays put Base model and quantized variants Base model Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning ). pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained( "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" ) pipe.load_components(dtype={ "vae" : torch.float32, "default" : torch.bfloat16}) pipe.to( "cuda" ) pipe.guider = pipe.guider.new(guidance_scale= 5.0 ) # optional image = pipe(prompt=prompt, output= "images" )[ 0 ] Single-file format checkpoints Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4 . Load any of them with from_single_file , then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too. from diffusers import BFLQuantizationConfig, Flux3Transformer2DModel, ModularPipeline model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" variant = "fp8r" # or "nvfp4" transformer = Flux3Transformer2DModel.from_single_file( f"https://huggingface.co/ {model_id} /blob/main/variants/ {variant} /model.safetensors" , config=model_id, subfolder= "transformer" , quantization_config=BFLQuantizationConfig(compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16), dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id) pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) pipe.update_components(transformer=transformer) pipe.to( "cuda" ) For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config . Variant Fast kernels on Other GPUs fp8r Compute capability 8.9+ (Ada, Hopper, Blackwell) Weights are dequantized each step: lower memory, no speedup nvfp4 Blackwell, with flashinfer-python and flashinfer-cubin at the same version Same as above LoRA finetuning FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit ). Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd : accelerate launch train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein.py \ --pretrained_model_name_or_path= "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" \ --dataset_name= "multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain" \ --caption_column= "caption" \ --instance_prompt= "trtcrd" \ --output_dir= "trained-flux3-tarot-lora" \ --mixed_precision= "bf16" \ --resolution=1024 \ --use_aspect_ratio_buckets \ --train_batch_size=1 \ --rank=16 \ --lora_alpha=16 \ --learning_rate=1e-4 \ --lr_scheduler= "constant" \ --max_train_steps=1500 \ --validation_prompt= "a trtcrd of a cat, tarot style" \ --validation_epochs=25 \ --seed=0 \ --push_to_hub To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags: --gradient_checkpointing \ --cache_latents \ --use_8bit_adam --gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit. A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora . More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README . For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script ( train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py ) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as <ref_image_0> . See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example. What it costs to run In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models. Memory name peak allocated (after load) GiBs peak allocated (after inference) GiBs nvfp4 (RTX6000) 13.4 15.3 fp8r (H100) 14.35 16.27 bf16 (H100) 18.80 20.72 If you have less memory: Load a quantized transformer . Run the text encoder separately and free it. It only runs once per image, before denoising (see Encode once, generate many ). Turn on automatic CPU offloading, which moves each component to the GPU only while it runs (we didn't benchmark this) from diffusers import ComponentsManager, ModularPipeline manager = ComponentsManager() manager.enable_auto_cpu_offload(device= "cuda" ) pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained( "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein" , components_manager=manager) pipe.load_components(dtype={ "vae" : torch.float32, "default" : torch.bfloat16}) # no pipe.to("cuda"): the manager handles device placement Speed End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup: Workflow Output size Time Peak memory Text-to-image 1024 × 1024 1.93 s 23.8 GiB Image-to-image, one 1024 × 1024 reference 1024 × 1024 3.87 s 23.8 GiB Layout editing (the knight), one 1360 × 768 reference 1360 × 768 4.10 s 23.8 GiB Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend. A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call Stacked bars of tokens per transformer call: text-to-image 4,256 tokens; image-to-image 8,272; layout text-to-image 4,336; layout image-to-image 8,800 The architecture Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens: text the noisy image being generated and optional reference images From pixels to tokens FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2. The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels. So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch , and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size. From prompt to tokens The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072. This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call. Two stages The transformer processes the tokens in two stages: Stage 1: per-mode blocks. Each stream goes through 5 blocks with its own weights. Text has its own blocks, the noisy image has its own, and the reference images have their own. Stage 2: joint blocks. The streams are concatenated into one sequence, [text | image | reference] , which goes through 28 blocks that share one set of weights. The two stages differ in who can attend to whom . In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them. At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image. Inside one block Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream. Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation ). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below. In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate. def block ( x, shift, scale, gate ): # shift, scale, gate come from the token's timestep embedding h = layer_norm(x) # no learned scale or shift h = ( 1 + scale) * h + shift q, k, v = to_q(h), to_k(h), to_v(h) q, k = rope(rms_norm(q)), rope(rms_norm(k)) out = attention(q, k, v) + mlp(h) # parallel, MLP is SwiGLU return x + gate * out Every token gets its own timestep In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token. The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t . The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0 , which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate. The distilled checkpoint is a flow map . It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump. Positions in four dimensions Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head: Tokens t: timestep h: height w: width l: length of sequence text token i 0 0 0 i image token at (row, col) 0 row / 2 col / 2 0 reference k at (row, col) 0 row / 2 col / 2 −( k + 1) Text tokens line up along l , like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w) , separated from each other along l . Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on. The denoising loop FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity . This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it. At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape: Step 1 Step 5 Step 10 Step 15 Step 25 Step 50 The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers. If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works. Modular Diffusers FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline. See the workflows You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights. from diffusers import Flux3AutoBlocks blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks() print (blocks.available_workflows) # ['text2image', 'image_conditioned'] print ( list (blocks.get_workflow( "text2image" ).sub_blocks)) # ['text_encoder', 'denoise.input', 'denoise.prepare_latents', 'denoise.set_timesteps', # 'denoise.prepare_rope_inputs', 'denoise.denoise', 'denoise.after_denoise', 'decode'] get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow. Encode once, generate many Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings. import torch from diffusers import ModularPipeline model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" blocks = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id).blocks text_blocks = blocks.sub_blocks.pop( "text_encoder" ) # `blocks` now starts at the VAE encoder text_pipe = text_blocks.init_pipeline(model_id) text_pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) text_pipe.to( "cuda" ) state = text_pipe(prompt=prompt, negative_prompt= "" ) # no guider here, so ask for the negative embeddings prompt_embeds = state.get( "prompt_embeds" ) negative_prompt_embeds = state.get( "negative_prompt_embeds" ) del text_pipe torch.cuda.empty_cache() image_pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id) # no text encoder to load image_pipe.load_components(dtype={ "vae" : torch.float32, "default" : torch.bfloat16}) image_pipe.to( "cuda" ) for seed in range ( 3 ): image = image_pipe( prompt_embeds=prompt_embeds, negative_prompt_embeds=negative_prompt_embeds, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed), output= "images" , )[ 0 ] image.save( f" {seed} .png" ) Add a step inside the loop The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step: from diffusers.modular_pipelines import Flux3AutoBlocks, InputParam, ModularPipelineBlocks, OutputParam class Flux3PreviewStep ( ModularPipelineBlocks ): model_name = "flux3" @property def inputs ( self ): return [InputParam( "latents" ), InputParam( "noise_pred" )] @property def intermediate_outputs ( self ): return [OutputParam( "x0_previews" , type_hint= list )] @torch.no_grad() def __call__ ( self, components, block_state, i, t ): if i == 0 : block_state.x0_previews = [] sigma = t / 1000 # timesteps are sigmas scaled to [0, 1000] block_state.x0_previews.append(block_state.latents - sigma * block_state.noise_pred) # x0 = x_t - sigma * v return components, block_state blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks() denoise_loop = blocks.sub_blocks[ "denoise" ].sub_blocks[ "text2image" ].sub_blocks[ "denoise" ] denoise_loop.sub_blocks.insert( "preview" , Flux3PreviewStep(), 1 ) # between "denoiser" and "after_denoiser" pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id) pipe.load_components(dtype={ "vae" : torch.float32, "default" : torch.bfloat16}) pipe.to( "cuda" ) out = pipe(prompt=prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output=[ "x0_previews" , "images" ]) Try it Models: FLUX.3 Image Klein collection Docs: FLUX.3 in Diffusers Fine-tune: DreamBooth LoRA scripts Prompting: Black Forest Labs prompting guide Built something with FLUX.3? items.title: The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself Published October 8, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 63 +57 yuvraj sharma ysharma Follow Abubakar Abid abidlabs Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern , and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16. Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware. How I prompt ML Intern The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts , exactly as I wrote them. A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky. Two lines in the prompt are critical . The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run. At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer. You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days. 1. A model that knows your field A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand. On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90. Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App 2. A model that draws your character Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B , trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset. The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model . From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60. Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App 3. A model that does a new trick Camera-angle LoRAs are among the most-liked community add-ons for earlier Qwen-Image models. You can give the model a picture of an object and ask to see it 45 degrees from the left. When I checked a few days after the Qwen-Image 2.1 model release, nobody had made one, so I tasked ML-intern to build it. ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions. Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App Doodle-in LoRA is another cool idea. Upload a photo with a magenta scribble on it and add a short prompt naming an object. The LoRA replaces the scribble with that object while keeping the original lighting and composition consistent. No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely. Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500. Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24. Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App 4. A model that fits your device The Pocket Rewriter from the top of this post is the first one. ML-intern started by generating 8,797 short image requests with a small instruct model through Inference Providers, following a mix set in my prompt: photos, posters, logos, infographics and more, about a third of them asking for exact text in quotes, and many in languages other than English. The 9B teacher then rewrote all of them on one A100 in 2 hours 37 minutes (~USD 6.50). After filtering for quality, 1,840 examples were selected for training dataset. Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena Agate-Preview-002-4step is the second. Logolabs' Agate Preview 002 is a 260M-parameter text-to-image model, small enough for a browser, but it needs 50 steps with guidance, which is 100 network passes per image. I asked ML-intern to distill it down to just 4 passes! It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22. I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37. Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE What it cost Model Base model Compute Citrus Doctor Qwen3.5-2B USD 1.90 Huggy LoRA FLUX.2 klein base 4B USD 7.60 Pocket rewriter (0.8B and 2B) Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B USD 16.05 Viewpoint Orbit LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 16 Doodle-in LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 24.30 Agate 4-step (two runs) Agate Preview 002 USD 37 Total about USD 103 These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session. Make yours ML-intern is in HuggingChat . Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap. If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace . We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.
